Driving works very well and the game allows you to purchase and acquire several cool vehicles.

Overall, you won’t regret playing this game if you haven’t already.

[h1]~Chippin In~ my thoughts[/h1]
For years, I avoided cyberpunk because of its infamous launch. I always figured that it had nothing to offer, considering the game launched as a buggy mess. However, like most people know at this point, cyberpunk has improved itself since half a decade ago when it launched in 2020.
During that time, a lot of people gave this game a second chance and ended up really resonating with it. Lots of my friends as well as people I respect really love Cyberpunk 2077. And because I wrote it off after launch, I never understood why people liked it so much. However, earlier this year a friend of mine bought me the game. So I finally decided to give it a try and find out why 2077 is so beloved nowadays.
50 hours, and 1 playthrough later I can comfortably say Cyberpunk 2077 mostly lives up to the hype. I wouldn't call it "an all-time great" but I would say it's a great game that has a lot to say about its subject matter.

[h2]+ Night City is a Captivating Setting[/h2]
The strongest part of Cyberpunk 2077 is easily its setting. In this game you play as V, an edgerunner and you work in Night City, a cyberpunk “utopia”. Compared to other RPG settings, Night City is a pretty great place to set your game. NC is brimming with corporate overlords, gangs, and outlaws that makes it perfect for an open world RPG. Furthermore, being an edgerunner means you have infinite potential for quests. Cyberpunk does a great job of taking advantage of these concepts. This isn't the first game to make a cyberpunk outlaw story seem cool. But 2077 definitely knows how to do this idea right.
Even the simple act of driving through Night City is so cool. Cyberpunk does everything in its power to make you feel like you're in the beating heart of this city. I found the whole experience really engaging. There are few games that I've played that make me feel such a connection to the world like Cyberpunk did. 

[h2]+ The Storyline/Major Quests were better than expected[/h2]
When I first started hearing about Cyberpunk, I heard a lot of praise for its storyline and side quests. So I was excited to see what all the hype was about. Though admittedly my expectations were pretty low. However, I was really surprised at how good the main story/quests were! The start of the main story is pretty weak. It's mostly just set up for the larger story the game is trying to tell. But once you get to the end of the first act, the story picks up in a major way. The stakes of the main story were really engaging. The arcs of the main characters were enthralling to me. And the themes of the story: death, the consequences of clinging to life, legacy. They're all done excellently.
On a different note, I really loved the major pieces of side content. The game presents you with lots of side quests that spin off of the main story. And I think these are excellent too. The major characters you meet throughout these quests, their arcs and plot lines that you follow throughout their quest lines. It's all excellent stuff. And you won't really miss any of the best quest lines because they're presented to you very blatantly.
I have some issues with the smaller quests that I mention later, as well as some problems with the game itself that affect the story in small ways. But overall I love the story/quests as presented and it's definitely one of the strongest elements of Cyberpunk.

[h2]- Majority of "minor content" is disappointing[/h2]
With the exception of the main story and major side quests, and some of the minor jobs. The side content of Cyberpunk is very disappointing to me. And I want to emphasize this because during my playthrough, I wanted to hit max level before I finished the game. So I was hoping that the side content would be a fun way to hit max level while seeing what else Cyberpunk had to offer. Unfortunately, this aspect ended up underwhelming me and I found this extremely disappointing, doubly so considering how good the main content was.
There are many side activities in 2077, the two major types being: gigs and NCPD Missions.
The gigs are the most plentiful type of side content. Contextually speaking, these quests are cool from a world-building perspective. And they give you something to do in Night City. But my issue is that the gigs are extremely formulaic. Most missions follow the same format: "Go into building, kill everyone/sneak around, find object, leave." That means as you're doing these quests, you're basically just doing the same thing over and over again. Which gets really old.
NCPD Missions are less common than gigs, but they're more boring and even more formulaic. You will randomly receive police scanner missions through the game that literally just amount to a random encounter with some thugs. It's extremely boring and I almost never engaged with this aspect of the game. Because it was just more pointless combat. Which this game has in abundance.

[h2]- The RPG mechanics lack depth[/h2]
My biggest issue with Cyberpunk are the RPG mechanics. If I were to make a thesis statement for my thoughts about Cyberpunk, I would say this: "Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game that cares far too much about killing people for some reason."
In Cyberpunk, every stat and perk you take is for combat, and only combat. Skill trees unlock new combat abilities, and passive perks; stats only exist to unlock perks and buff combat damage. The game's RPG mechanics are for combat, first and foremost. And unfortunately the combat itself is nothing special. It's the Bethesda special of hitting/shooting something until it dies. There's some sauce in there too: cyber implants, hacking, and admittedly fun perks add some variety to gameplay. But for the most part you're just shooting and hitting things. Which gets old, especially considering that's the only way you can solve most quests.
The unfortunate truth of Cyberpunk's quest design is that your two options are "Murder? Or Murder quietly". The few times the game gives you the option to avoid violence are few and far between, though there are moments in there that give you the option. But it's never anything substantial or deeply rewarding.
To be fair, there are moments where the game offers the player opportunities to pick dialogue options based on your stats. These actually influence the quest you're doing or let you choose a different outcome for a quest because of how you built your character. But these moments aren't common, and are usually just recontextualizing a different outcome you could've gotten otherwise. Overall, there doesn't feel like there are many meaningful ways for the way you built V to affect the game outside of combat. Obviously, there are exceptions to this, like I mentioned. But I spent most of the game wishing that player interaction based on your decisions with the game was the rule, not the exception.
The short-sighted decision to not let the player use their stats to "role-play" in this "role-playing game" is so disappointing to me. It's such a shame too, because you can see moments where the game tries to do this. But these moments are few and far between. More like fun easter eggs, and not intentional design decisions.
It's such a shame because the game is begging for this depth. I really hope a sequel doesn't shy away from the depth that a truly great RPG can offer.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
In its current state, Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game. The story has a lot to say, and the combat is serviceable. And Night City is a setting that will likely stay in my memory for years to come. But its lack of depth in aspects that matter to me left me with a dissatisfied feeling after the credits rolled. So I can't say that this game is incredible, like some people have told me it is.
I think it's a 4/5 in my book. A great game, with major flaws that hold it back. But its best elements won't fade away in my mind any time soon.

One of my favorite games of all time. I did not play it when it first launced broken, but they have absolutely turned it into a masterpeice. As of writing this i spent 131 hours on my first playthrough only. And it feels like i barely scratched the surface of all the extremely high quality content this game has to offer. 

Gameplay:
It is such a fun game. The combat feels really good with both guns and blades. I used a katana and knife on my first playthrough and did stealth were i could. Both flet really fun. Blades, knifes and guns all feel amazing and the combat is fastpaced and so fun. I will do my next playthrough (whenever that is) using a netrunner build, becuase that also looks really fun. The cars and bikes are also really nice in this game. And the progression feels really great with lots of options and fun upgrades without feeling grindy. And even though the mainstory is kinda short, there is a RIDICULOUS amount of amazing side quests (hence my 131 hour long first playthrough).

Story:
Wont write too much about its details too avoid spoilors, but it is one of the best i have played through. All the characters feel really human, having their own streangths and flaws. The animations are topnotch and really bring them to life. I highly recommend buying the dlc Phamtom Liberty, wich not only ads ever more content to the gameplay but also some of the best writing in the game. I nearly cried at the end of Phamtom Libery as well as the end of the base game.

Graphics:
One of the best looking games ever, if your hardware can handle it. I have quite a beefy pc wich let me play the game on highest settings with stable 30 fps, but it might (understatement) be demanding for lower end systems. It also has a kinda low drawdistance on things like cars, wich become somewhat noticeble png's when far away. Its not a big problem, and there are mods to fix it, but still. But fancy ligthing and car png's aside, this game has a amazing artstyle with vibrant colors and cool designs on everything from buildings, weapons and characters.

Music:
Just great. Way too many radiostations to listen to when being a traffic menace.

Conclusion:
Buy it if your system can handle the graphics. Otherwise i hope you will someday be able to experiance this game. If your system can handle it, buy Phamtom Liberty as well and watch the anime Edgerunners.

Cyberpunk 2077 is more than just a game—it’s an unforgettable experience. Night City is one of the most immersive and beautifully designed worlds I’ve ever explored. Every street, building, character, and neon-lit corner feels alive, making the city itself feel like a character in the story.
The story is incredible, emotional, and full of memorable characters. V’s journey, the choices you make, and the relationships you build genuinely pulled me into the world. And Johnny Silverhand is one of those characters you simply don’t forget.
The atmosphere, soundtrack, visuals, combat, character customization, and attention to detail all come together perfectly. There were moments when I stopped playing just to look around and appreciate how much detail was put into Night City.
Cyberpunk 2077 is the kind of game that stays with you even after you finish it. It has flaws, but the overall experience is something truly special.
After everything I experienced in Night City, my rating is simple:
10/10 — Absolute masterpiece.

Very mixed feelings overall. Before playing I had heard everyone say "the game is fixed now after the bad launch" and that makes me wonder just how bad it must have been at launch because it is still incredibly unstable. Random bugs, crashes, and visual errors are still absolutely everywhere. You can only get flashbanged every time you close your map so many times before it really starts hurting the experience.

Visually the game is mostly great. The environments and general art direction are phenomenal, all of the districts are distinct from each other and its easy to tell where you are just based on the aesthetics of your area. I found myself rarely using fast travel because of how much I enjoyed just driving around on the motorcycles (i wish the cars controlled as well as the bikes do.) The only bad thing I can say here is that outside of the main cast every character looks like they're made of plastic and they usually have extremely out of sync vocal animations. The NPCs are probably the weakest part of this game. The random outfits make most of them look stupid and their dialogue is vapid and repetitive. Nothing kills immersion quite like a dude with no jaw talking to you in regular english. I found it hilarious when I was in the aldecaldo camp and like 80% of the people there were random NPCs who would still give you the hostile dialogues if you talked to them even though you're supposed to be like family by that point. There's also a very small amount of NPC templates so it's not uncommon to see like 4 of the same guy in one place. If you're thinking about ray tracing I would just do ray traced reflections as it's the only one that's worth the frame loss in my opinion (seriously ray traced lighting makes most areas look worse and drops my frames by like 50fps)

The gunplay is fine, there's not much to say about it. Standard weapon archetypes, though long range options are very limited. Precision rifles generally suck and snipers are really slow, clunky and hard to come by. Most encounters rely on numbers over individual power so snipers are usually useless. This game really wants you to be aggressive at all times, there's a whole stealth tutorial section that feels pointless because there's no reason to ever be stealthy because bum rushing them with a shotgun is the best option 9/10 times. It doesn't help that the enemy AI is really really stupid, the vast majority of enemies just stand there and wait for you to kill them. The few that actually have unique attack patterns are used sparsely and even then its usually some kind of repetitive super speed melee attack. The smasher boss fight is genuinely the only fight I can say I actually found myself interested in. Mantis blades are cool but you're not given much incentive to use them because again in 9/10 situations a shotgun does what they do but better. Movement can also be pretty clunky until you get some of the later upgrades.

The story is inconsistent. The quality massively varies between storylines. Every side mission feels like an afterthought. Everything surrounding Arasaka directly just feels confused. Maybe I just took a bad route or something but by the end it feels like the writers just forgot that this game was originally about taking down Arasaka. A good chunk of the story was about trying to get to Hanako to expose Yorinobu and once you actually get to her she basically just goes "I'll handle it" and it gets dropped. The dynamic with Johnny is interesting but it entirely takes over the story by the end. These 2 storylines were both set up at the start but only 1 of them had a satisfying conclusion. This game is rich thematically but the plot generally doesn't inform those themes and at worst directly contradicts them. Cyberpunk really wants to "say something" but it isn't exactly sure what it wants to say or how to say it. This game is marketed as a "choose your own adventure" game but most dialogue options either don't change the outcome of an interaction or it's 3 "different" dialogues that all mean the same thing. It's hard to tell what's actually going to affect the story and what won't. 

This game starts out very strong but the more I played the harder I found it to keep going. It kinda just stops introducing new mechanics after the interlude. The main storylines are pretty engaging but basically every side mission is mind numbingly boring and pointless. Cyberpunk loves having huge dramatic moments for characters that it didn't put the effort into getting you to care about. There were so many times where I was clearly meant to be feeling something and I was just sitting there thinking to myself "who is this again?" It really makes me wonder what was happening behind the scenes considering how long this game took to make. 

TLDR: It's a decent game. 6/10. I'd wait for a sale.

This game is undoubtedly a work of art. 
Despite Night City's bleak and rather dystopian atmosphere, it manages to feel alive, purposeful, everything is there (mostly) for a reason, you will drive around and just randomly feel awe that a world like this was brought to life in a game. The story manages to deliver in every possible way, feelings were brought out that I never even thought I could experience. 

The main story is compelling, it hooks you in immediately and may defy your expectations at many junctures throughout, and every optional gig and occasional detour is special, it's not surprising to find yourself off-track on some new adventure or in the middle of many Night City rabbit-holes. It truly allows you to ask yourself how YOU want to do this, how you want to experience this story, and what path you want to tread on.  

Keanu Reeve's performance as Johnny Silverhand is one of my favorite things about this game, your bond with this character goes unimaginable lengths, I'm forever grateful for how much work was put into making this character this impactful and well written. Cherami Leigh gave us one of the best voice acting performances for a protagonist, and Minji Chang as Song So Mi was able to steal the spotlight whenever she appeared despite performing alongside Idris Elba. 

The expansion is everything you could ask for and more. Phantom Liberty is a spy thriller (with the chance to turn into an Alien Isolation-esque horror game) that presents you with amazing characters and difficult choices, every decision matters, and none of them are easy. The rollercoaster of manipulation, lies, trauma, and tension will leave you either staring blankly at the screen or sobbing by the time the credits roll. 

Whilst the launch has left a bitter taste, the efforts of the many talented individuals that worked towards making this an unforgettable experience have not been in vain. I really hope more people give this game a second chance. 
I'm excited for Cyberpunk 2, and you should be too.

Look. I know a lot has been said about this game, both good and bad. I'm not breaking new ground here. The pros of this game are the immaculate vibes and graphics. Being locked in on a mission makes the game flow and can be, at times, fun. And if this game was just an on-the-rail story-driven FPS, then yeah, I wouldn't have much to complain about (besides the hard crashes and game-breaking bugs that are still rampant, even now). 

The thing is, I can't let what happened be excused. I know CDPR pulled a "NMS" here and spent the last few years fixing it up, and that's good. But to glaze this game now only excuses the absolute fact that not only did they sell me an unplayable mess at start, they also sold me a DIFFERENT GAME. I pre-ordered this game because the makers of TW3 promised me an OPEN WORLD RPG, just like TW3, but cyberpunk. That is not what this game is. Night City is empty, a vacuous window-dressing void of any and all content save for the rare "work for the police by killing some dudes" (in a "punk" game, you sure do spend a lot of time doing the police's dirty work). No factions, no meaningful choices, all the shops and doors are closed, I could go on and on. Walking around NC is fun for the vibes, but it gets incredibly boring, and then depressing. 

I wanted to love this game so much. I was ready to lose myself in it. But even after waiting years to get this game in a playable state, it's clear this game is not 'open world' in any meaningful sense. It's not a 'role playing game' beyond choosing your combat style. Nothing you do really matters. Hop in a car (which are still absurdly hard to control on mouse/keyboard) and all the lights turn green, all the traffic disappears. Nothing you do matters, in the open world or in the story missions, as everything leads to a single "pick your ending" moment. In some ways, I'm more disappointed now than I was on launch.

If you want to just hang out in a cool futuristic cyberpunk city, this is the game for that. If you love story-driven on-the-rails FPS games, this is a great game for that. But if you want an open world role playing game, I can assure you that this is not that game. Don't reward bad corpo behavior, choom. Stop glazing this still-buggy mess of a failed promise.

Genuinely one of the best games I've ever played. I was skeptical at first, but it's really up there with The Witcher 3 as one of the most memorable titles in this genre.

Now, I don't know how broken or buggy it was during its initial launch, but the Cyberpunk 2077 I played this year ended up being a breathtakingly immersive experience packed full of content that makes you wanna keep coming back for more, all set in a world that feels genuinely alive, right down to the most minute details; where even the optional side quests are well-crafted, offering intriguing and thought-provoking side-narratives filled with moral ambiguity in a dystopian world of ruthless megacorps and rampant body augmentation.

Combat is both fun and flashy, and once you unlock some perks and level up, the game leans heavily into providing an absolute power trip of an experience where you become this ultra-augmented beast of a merc who can take down entire armies on their own. Night City is also one of the most impressively detailed open worlds I've seen in a while; it feels great to just get lost on its bustling, neon-lit streets, completing gigs and side missions while always finding something new and exciting around the next corner. Aside from a few hiccups here and there, everything feels insanely believable, and the immersion is impeccable.

So yeah, if you want to play an excellent futuristic first-person action-RPG, this is the one to pick. And make sure to grab Phantom Liberty as well, as it adds a sizable new zone to explore in the form of Dogtown, along with several new side quests and a main storyline that I personally found to be better than the base game's. Also, don't wait until the endgame to start it; just jump in the moment it’s unlocked and finish it before returning to the main game's narrative. At least that's what I'd recommend.

It's often said that the mark of a great game is that you'll keep thinking about it even when you're not actively playing it, and I’d say Cyberpunk 2077 most definitely falls into that category. It ended up being one of the best gaming experiences I've had in a long while, and I seriously cannot recommend it enough.

While each aspect of this game is phenomenal, for me the writing is where the game truly shines: character dialogue is intentional and impactful, and the voice actor's are all up to the task when it comes to conveying that emotional impact to the player. The plot is interesting and engaging, and the art, design, and atmosphere is the best in the genre, bar none. Mike Pondsmith's lore and worldbuilding is exquisitely rich and provides a unique and interesting interpretation of retrofuturism, and CDPR did a great job creating the perfect video game adaptation of that world. Player choices, both dialogue and actual actions, feel like they influence the outcome of storylines in a way that few games are able to accomplish. The score and sound design are also great and compliment the world perfectly. Despite the vast and detailed world, the performance is also fairly good, despite the issues at launch. I did encounter a handful of bugs during my time with the game, but nothing egregious and no more frequently than other AAA titles I've played recently. 

And despite the base game being absolutely excellent, CDPR totally outdid themselves with Phantom Liberty, which is the perfect compliment to what was already a great cyberpunk game. If you don't have or haven't tried the DLC, I cannot recommend it enough. It provides nearly as much content as the base game, and all of the content is even better than what was provided in the base game. It is seriously one of the best implementations of paid DLC in a single player game I've ever seen, the only game that I can think of that compares is Mass Effect 3. This won't be a carefully put-together review, no. I feel like I closed a chapter with my last playthrough, and I just want to dump every single thought I had while playing this game.

First, I want to say that despite all the mean things I will mention, I really, really love this game. It is absolutely on another level. Not to mention the path it went through: from being an absolute atrocity at launch to becoming a fan-favorite gem. Cyberpunk 2077 is the only game I can play for 200+ hours and not get bored. On the contrary, 200+ hours just makes me want to play it more and NEVER meet Hanako at Embers. I feel like everything I went through on my journey made me close to V. Characters, story, jokes, interactions - all of it is so dear to me, and it makes Cyberpunk 2077 one of my favorite games ever.

Ok, sentiments aside, let's break it down:

I ABSOLUTELY LOVE V's voice. Both male and female. Gavin Drea and Cherami Leigh gave us a textbook example of great voice acting and immersion into a character. In most RPGs, your character feels like an avatar. But V is an actual person. Not only do you have three lifepaths that actually change V's attitude towards some things, but the character themselves has their own opinions and views on things - to mention one: V thinks the Mizutani Shion is a car for flash-posers. It is a small detail, but it just adds to the immersion that V is a real person. And there are A LOT of small details like that.

Cyberpunk 2077 is truly an open world. The game lets you explore up and down, far and wide. I adore games that let you get to places you were clearly not supposed to reach. In Cyberpunk, you can literally climb buildings with the right perks and cyberware. Damn, you can even climb Arasaka Tower if you want to. I did it in my last playthrough. Although it kinda feels like a side effect of rushed development - they just didn't have enough time to add invisible walls to prevent you from getting out of bounds, etc., because in Phantom Liberty there are a lot fewer places you can climb to and a lot more invisible walls. But what we have is pretty nice. I had a lot of fun just jumping around the city, wondering if it was possible to climb that next building.

Talking about the city... Night City is one of the most alive-feeling cities I've ever encountered in video games. In most games, NPCs just walk around and don't have any life to them. But if you take a slow stroll around Night City, you will feel its heart (a very dark one at that). Encounters, points of interest, the aftermath of deals gone wrong, weird and funny posters that you would never see if you sped by in a car. Simple citizens existing, lives turned into nightmares, people escaping reality through braindances and drugs, and MANY, MANY more things. All of that adds up to the aliveness of the in-game world.

No matter what localization you have, people will speak THEIR language and you will see subtitles. I absolutely love when games do that. I can't quite explain it, but it adds A TON to the immersion.

The music is BANGER after BANGER in this game. The original soundtrack is breathtaking, and some songs will stay with you forever. They will chip into your brain and never fade away from your memory. You're gonna really want to stay at your house just to listen to those god-tier tracks. Not only that, but the fact that CDPR hired a band and created SAMURAI is just nuts to me. Most developers prefer to stick to famous rappers and mainstream singers, so I'm very glad that a band like that got such a huge shoutout.

Very cool easter eggs in this game. Especially FF:06:B5. Iykyk. Mind-blowing, I would say. The finale of that one literally made me leave my house and go on a very long and very silent stroll, contemplating life. Thanks.

AMAZING mod compatibility. I was rocking my last playthrough with 355 mods, and the game worked perfectly. Very few unprovoked crashes and great stability. Huge props to CDPR and modders. Impeccable job.

Now, unfortunately, we move on to things that are not so bright and are sometimes straight-up bad. Well, nobody is perfect. Here I go:

The story is very short. Its quality and depth kinda make up for its length, but still, you know, I was expecting much more from the pacing. I thought Jackie would play a bigger part in the story. Instead of spending time developing his character and his bond with V, they turned it into a "6 months montage." Not only that, but they [spoiler] straight-up spoiled his death in the 2019 E3 trailer. I thought it was one of the POSSIBLE outcomes, but no. [/spoiler] The game is pretty linear. Most of your choices don't matter in the bigger picture. Consider them your role-playing options. Cool detail, but not what we were promised.

Even though Cyberpunk went through a lot of positive technical improvements, some things stayed the same and remained straight-up ignored:
Some animations look like they're from the '90s, sounds are out of sync, enemy behavior is weird, and some scenes have detailed sound design while others are completely silent even though there obviously should be sounds. Ok, the game is from 2020, most people were sitting at home and motion capture was unavailable. I get it.

Cyberpunk looks amazing without the interface, but unfortunately, it is not meant to be played that way. It's not optimized for it at all because you have no idea what you need to interact with or where to go.
There is also forced parking near certain characters. Like, I get it, it is there to prevent players from ramming into people, but come on, it is a role-playing game, so let me role-play and park on the side of the road.

Updates brought us romance hangouts. But even with mods, they are extremely boring and uninspired. No new dialogue options, they play out the same every time, and they don't feel interesting or intimate at all.

Lastly, I was expecting more from the in-game cyberware. There was a CGI trailer that included a chrome installation animation which, of course, is not present in the game. And also, the fact that some cyberware acts like simple perks - "adds 10% mitigation chance" - feels very underwhelming for a combat implant.

That's it. Once again, I want to say that it IS a great game. An amazing game. Top-tier. Despite everything. There are not enough words in human languages to fully describe how much I love it. If you haven't tried it for yourself yet, man, you are in for a treat.

I had to give Cyberpunk 2077 a second shake.

The first time I played it, I genuinely thought it just wasn't my kind of game. I wasn't invested, the story wasn't grabbing me, and I actually fell asleep during the unskippable diner scene with Goro Takemura. After that, I couldn't really bring myself to keep playing.

Eventually, though, I came back. I figured the game deserved a fair chance, and I'm genuinely glad I gave it one.

Cyberpunk 2077 is amazing.

It still has its quirks from time to time. I've had quests bug out, the vehicle autodrive decide it has absolutely no idea where it's going, and occasionally my car just refuses to be summoned. But those are complaints I'm sure players have been hearing in one form or another since the game released.

What really won me over was the freedom. I love the build crafting and how differently you can approach combat. I love being able to explore Night City, wander off somewhere completely unrelated to the main story, and just do my own thing. Most importantly, I enjoy being given choices that actually feel like they belong in this world. There isn't always one obvious "right" answer, and there shouldn't be.

Night City is a place where almost nothing can be trusted, everyone seems to have an angle, and sometimes you're choosing between bad, worse, and whatever lets you sleep at night. Do what you think is right. Or don't. I'm not judging. It's your playthrough.

That's also what I've come to appreciate about V. V can be whoever you want them to be. You decide how they look, how they fight, what they believe, who they trust, who they love, who they help, and who they absolutely ruin.

My first impression of Cyberpunk 2077 was completely wrong. I thought it was slow, uninteresting, and simply wasn't for me. Turns out I just hadn't given Night City enough time to sink its claws into me. It deserved that second chance. And now I'm hooked.

Cyberpunk 2077 is simply a masterclass in atmosphere and player agency, and it finally feels like the definitive RPG experience it was meant to be. Running this game on an OLED display with path tracing cranked up makes the streets of Night City look absolutely gorgeous. Every single midnight drive through those neon-drenched districts is incredibly immersive. The map itself might not have the widest geographical footprint compared to some other sprawling open-world titles, but it feels incredibly massive because of how remarkably dense and multi-layered the city actually is. Getting lost in the intense verticality of the megabuildings and stumbling onto highly unique weapons tucked away in off-the-beaten paths was easily one of the most rewarding parts of my playthrough.

What really hooked me, though, is how the game handles physical progression. Having your cyberware act as your core armor and stats completely reinvents the usual RPG loot grind. Every trip to the ripperdoc feels like a monumental shift in how you play. When you pair that hardware with the highly specialized perk trees, you can actually carve out a very distinct build identity rather than just generically leveling up a jack-of-all-trades.

I committed to a Katana and Sandevistan build, and the traversal mechanics unlocked by those cyberware upgrades turned every single encounter into a kinetic, bloody blur. It completely breaks the mold of a standard first-person shooter. The boss fights are genuinely fun across the board, but the final showdown against Adam Smasher was the absolute peak of the game's combat. Triggering the Sandevistan to match his cybernetic speed felt exactly like two speedsters clashing in hyper-time—an insanely fast, high-octane duel that perfectly validated my entire build.

Beyond the sheer combat loop, taking the time to carve out a quiet life in the city really grounded the whole experience. Grinding out gigs to buy and own an impressive roster of cars and apartments gave me a tangible sense of progression, taking my V from a lowly street merc to a bonafide Night City legend. Taking all that hard-earned gear and riding out into the Badlands to finish out the Nomad path with Panam just felt like the perfect narrative payoff. It is a dense, brilliant game that actually lets you live in its world.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of, if not hands down the best game I've ever played. They did such an amazing job on the world building, it really made the game feel alive, like there was actual people outside of the player who existed.

For example, you can see the difference between a group like the Valentinos, which was a group built up on the fact that the area is poor so crime is going to happen, but they also had a (admittedly loose for real life) honour code, that valued their community, versus groups like Maelstrom which was essentially people who traded their morals for quick and easy pleasure. This works so well in terms of the world because nearly every person who inhabits the city is forced to make a decision, balancing survival with what they were willing to lose. And for those who push through, make it despite the odds being stacked against them, the best they can hope for is a job at a company that will treat them as a disposable pawn. There's a shard I remember reading during the The Star ending, that talks about the best companies to work for being ranked, and the best by a wide mile, truly blowing every other corp out of the water, gave a massive 5 days off a year, and had ONLY a 15 year mandatory working period.

It was extraordinarily easy to lose yourself in Night City, to start becoming used to how it functions, with homeless people, gangs, and murder on near enough every street corner. They are truly everywhere. There's 156 NCPD scanner hustles in the game and each one of them involves enough death and murder (either by the perpetrators or left behind by me) that it desensitizes you to how common place it is. What I think really builds up the world around you though, is a handful of the missions that stand out amongst the random chaos, the broad daylight executions.

Missions like "Sinnerman" in which a murderer claims he has repented, has turned to Christianity, and wants forgiveness from the family of a man he murdered. The reason this mission works so well is because you get to see the family, hear the grief in their voices. This mission really stuck with me not because of what it said, but because of what it didn't. The sister has forgiven him, while the mother has not, but the sisters forgiveness, it it real? Or is it simply a symptom of grief, of needing to make sense of the world around her, trying to pin meaning on her brothers senseless killing not as something that simply happened, unimportant to the world at large, but as an act of God, something that needed to happen to spread his word. And has he truly repented? Accepted God as his true divine purpose? He claims he has, but he is rattled very easily by a few questions against the actions he is taking. Prison in night city is stuff of nightmares, in a near literal sense, as prisoners are hooked up to machines that essentially force them to live and feel the most torturous sensations that have happened in the world, on a constant loop, forever. Does he truly feel remorse, or does he simply see an out to his never ending torture? We never get a clear answer.

Another mission that was truly telling of Night City, but in a different way, was "Dirty Biz". In this gig you need to simply find a BD that would solve the murder of a mans son. But at the end of the gig, you come across a father and son who put them together for sale, not the people who make them mind you. Looking at their messages you can see they peddle the worst of the worst, including animals/human, suicide, and children. The game give you options of how to handle the pair, and also arguments from the father on why you should spare them. The argument essentially comes down to 'If you kill us, we'll be replaced by others, who may be even worse'. Now by our standards, these people deserve immediate death, but this is Night City, a place where moral codes only exist for the people who died due to preserving them. And the argument makes sense, while they are clearly terrible people, they truly aren't amongst the worst we've met, just the ones who we know for a fact are involved. Personally I chose to kill the son, make the father live out his life knowing that what he did cost him the most important thing he had, but there's no correct answer. Leaving these people who are helping a horrible business exist alive doesn't feel right, but we don't know their circumstances, this may have truly been their only option, and killing them both means they will probably be replaced by worse people, people who enjoy the job. Given the fact that it's both son and father, the son probably never had any choice, this is what he was destined to do based on who his parents were, but does that means he shouldn't be punished? And given that he likely never had a choice, not truly, is killing his father, forcing him to live with losing him, truly just? Especially when most likely without him he will most likely either die, or have to join a gang with low enough standards to accept him, where he will almost certainly be forced to do far worse than what he already was.

Things like this gig are what really builds up Night City as a place of nightmares, where applying a moral code simply does not function, as anyone with one is destined to die, meaning no one ever has one, it's a snake eating its own tail.

Now onto some complaints:

The game, while nowhere near the pile of bugs and glitches it was at launch, is still unfortunately not as polished as one would hope and expect. Now there weren't many game breaking issues I came across, but there were certainly quite a few small, annoying ones. Some examples include a delamain car which never moved, and is still parked, blocking a street 100 hours later, I clipped through an elevator and got stuck during a mission, meaning I had to reload to an earlier save and lose my progress. Many visual glitches, such as the road not loading below my car. Weapons on cars refusing to come out, audio cutting out while in a car meaning i can't hear if im hitting anyone while shooting, auto drive going in circles, or driving straight into civilians then stopping, just a lot of the car stuff.

The only truly infuriating bug, that wasted a ton of my time and nearly drove me to giving up, was that the first mission of Phantom Liberty was glitched, and would not let me progress by interacting with an access point. I finally figured out that it was an issue with loading zones, so i ended up fast traveling away and running to the mission. This was the only time I truly considered this game as "bad", since I can accept that there's gonna be glitches, some that make me fail a mission or even have to reload to a previous save, but to have the FIRST MISSION of the PAID DLC so badly bugged that you can't even play it or progress, is frankly outrageous, and I can't believe that it still has not been fixed considering it's been around for years at this point.

I also have some more general complaints, such as a lot of the side content being, 'kill this person', 'steal this item', there was no real depth or stakes. Now I know not everything in the game can be fleshed out, but it felt like there was A LOT of missions and gigs that had so much potential, and ended up just being a single objective with nothing else around it. 

I also didn't like the NCPD at all, they are so laughably bad that I don't think there was a single point where I died to them, or even came close. To escape them all you have to do is drive away from them, but you can't really hide or outsmart them because they'll always know where you are, it's just a matter or them getting there before the timer runs out. You could take it as commentary on how the NCPD is so corrupt and swarmed by crime that they can only afford a small amount of time to each crime, but realistically I think its just Bad AI.

Despite these issues however, I have a lot of hope for the new cyberpunk game.

Cyberpunk 2077 launched in December 2020 with… let’s say “a few” issues, yet it still stands as one of the best games I’ve ever played. I didn’t preorder it or dive in on day one, but I’ll never forget firing it up on my Xbox and being greeted by a 50GB update. Meanwhile, the community was busy filling forums with complaints about performance, bugs, and everything in between.

Still, even the rough edges had their silver linings. Plenty of players took advantage of early glitches to rake in easy eddies — eurodollars, for anyone new to Night City. The most famous was the painting exploit, where you could repeatedly sell Untitled 18 – Brancesi, 2021 for 5,000 €$ using a drop point and the wait function. CD Projekt eventually shut it down — unsurprising, given how many YouTube videos were showcasing it.

Fast‑forward a bit, and the game eventually received countless bug fixes and, of course, the big 2.0 overhaul. When I returned for the Phantom Liberty DLC — long after completing the original story — it felt like a completely different game. So different, in fact, that I immediately switched off my Xbox and swore I’d never touch this (beep) game again.

Since then, life has done what life does. Much like the game’s protagonist, I’ve dealt with loss, prescription meds, and the kind of sleep deprivation only young children can inflict. I’ve found myself drifting back to the older games I used to love, mostly because I can’t afford to keep up with the current generation — and because my family mean far more to me than any AAA release ever will.

Thankfully, my Steam Deck has given my library a second life, letting me revisit a whole era of Xbox One and PS4 classics — Days Gone, Deus Ex: Human Revolution, God of War, Horizon: Zero Dawn, Spider‑Man, Quantum Break, Jedi: Fallen Order, Uncharted 4, and of course CD Projekt’s own The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.

Now, if you were put off by the 2.0 overhaul like I was, there’s good news: you can still play Cyberpunk 2077 using the 1.63 Legacy Patch — the final stable build from the 1.6 era before everything changed. If you’re a returning player, you can relive Cyberpunk 2077 in its original glory, and if you’re new and want to experience Night City as it was pre‑overhaul, you absolutely can. But there’s one catch: Phantom Liberty only works on the current, fully updated version, so consider that before choosing which build to commit to. To switch, just head into the game’s Properties, open the Game Versions & Betas section, and select 1_63_legacy_patch.

As for me, I played on the legacy patch for a while, completing around half the storyline, until curiosity finally got the better of me and I updated to the current public version. And honestly? I was surprised — pleasantly, even. But before switching, I made sure to grind out roughly 5,000,000 €$ to unlock the Autojock achievement. My method was simple and very Night City: max Technical Ability, grab the Ashura crafting spec, buy mountains of junk from the Jackson Plains vendor, craft Ashuras until your components cry for mercy, sell them at the drop point, wait 24 hours, and repeat until you’re a millionaire five times over.

It’s not glamorous, but neither is Night City. And hey, it works.

And speaking of Night City — welcome. A grand, chaotic, neon‑lit playground full of danger, opportunity, and legends waiting to be made. The game begins with a difficulty selection and then immediately asks you to choose a Lifepath: Nomad, Corpo, or Streetkid. Each one gives V an origin story and unlocks unique dialogue options throughout the game. Pick ten of these Lifepath‑tagged lines and you’ll unlock the Stanislavski’s Method achievement.

After that, you’re free to customise V however you like. The options are almost limitless: body type, skin tone, hairstyles, eye colour, facial structure, makeup, cyberware, scars, piercings, tattoos — you name it. And if you change your mind later, you can always adjust your appearance again.

Once your version of V is ready, you’ll allocate Attributes to shape your playstyle. Each Attribute governs specific skill trees, letting you build anything from a solo brawler to a stealthy ninja, a high‑tech netrunner, or a hybrid of all three. I personally went with a high‑damage netrunner setup — perfect for stealth and perfect for my millionaire‑times‑five scheme.

Being able to clear a room by firing off quickhacks through cameras — Short Circuit to knock enemies out, Synapse Burnout to finish them, Ping to map their positions, Distract Enemies to slip past unnoticed — felt incredibly satisfying. And if you want to go full MGS, invest in Optical Camo for temporary invisibility. But if you’d rather go in guns blazing, go full one‑man‑army — Schwarzenegger style. The choice is yours, and that’s the beauty of Night City.

After the prologue, you’ll find yourself restricted to Watson, one of the first districts you can freely roam. Even so, there’s plenty to keep you busy while the main story slowly opens up the rest of the city. You can take on gigs from Regina Jones, respond to NCPD scanner hustles, or simply explore and pick up anything that isn’t nailed down. Completing gigs and hustles is one of the best ways to rack up XP early on.

As you work through the first few missions, you’ll meet characters like Jackie Welles, Misty, Vic, Dexter Deshawn, and netrunner T‑Bug. Later on, you’ll encounter countless factions, corpos, fixers, and legends — including Keanu Reeves’ iconic Johnny Silverhand — all waiting for you to make your mark.

As for the game’s mechanics, whichever version you choose — legacy or 2.0 — the core combat remains very much the same. Your arsenal ranges from firearms to melee weapons to cyberware, with many ranged weapons supporting attachments such as silencers, muzzle brakes, and scopes. Smart weapons use gyrojet technology and onboard tracking to lock onto targets and even curve bullets around obstacles — but only if you’ve installed the Smart Link cyberware.

Alongside firearms, you’ll have a selection of bladed weapons, including futuristic katanas inspired by the game’s Japanese factions. Add cyberware like Mantis Blades — retractable forearm weapons designed for fast, lethal close‑quarters combat — and you can tailor your entire arsenal to your preferred fighting style.

For me, I’ve leaned heavily into smart weapons: the Ashura sniper rifle, Yinglong with its massive damage output and EMP explosions, and a silenced Unity — a compact .45‑caliber handgun with a high fire rate. I also keep The Headsman tucked away: a stockless variant of the Constitutional Arms M2038 shotgun, perfect for close‑quarters encounters when things get messy.

With more than enough content to keep you busy — from the base game to Phantom Liberty — you’ll easily rack up 150 hours of excitement. I’m currently sitting at 115 hours and still have plenty left to do.

At the end of the day, Cyberpunk 2077 is chaotic, stylish, loud, emotional, occasionally broken, frequently brilliant, and always fun. It’s the kind of game that makes you say “just one more gig” at 3AM and then wonder why the sun is rising. Whether you play the legacy build or the shiny new version, Night City delivers — and if you’re anything like me, you’ll be back for more long before your eddies dry up. It’s absolutely worth investing in. CD Projekt may have had a rough start, but Cyberpunk 2077 has grown into a truly amazing game.

A bit late to the party, but Cyberpunk 2077 is overall a great game, and after finally playing through it, I can see why people have been talking about this game for years.

[b]First, I'll start with the POSITIVES:[/b]
+ [b]Holy moly, the world and immersion are 10/10.[/b] Just taking a stroll through Night City is beautiful. Sometimes I completely forget about the objective and just explore.
+ [b]The story is overall solid.[/b] The first quarter with Jackie was a masterpiece and my favorite part. I'll leave the spoilers out, but it hooked me pretty quickly.
+ [b]The game runs great on my system.[/b] I'm getting around 50–70 FPS at 1440p on medium/high settings depending on where I am in the world.
+ [b]The characters actually feel unique.[/b] Most of the major characters have their own personality, style, and missions that make them stand out.
+ [b]Tons of customization.[/b] Guns, cars, clothes, stats, skills, perks, etc. There are plenty of ways to build your character around your own playstyle.
+ [b]Night City is just incredibly cool.[/b] The atmosphere, music, neon, architecture, and overall cyberpunk aesthetic are probably my favorite part of the game.

[b]Here are some NEGATIVES that come to mind:[/b]
- [b]Gunplay feels wonky at first.[/b] I can't really pinpoint what it is, but something about the shooting just felt off. You eventually get used to it though lol 
-[b] Some side missions feel like filler.[/b] At times the game turns into a glorified to-do list of "go here, kill these guys, loot, repeat."
- [b]The level cap surprised me.[/b] I had to Google why I was stuck at level 50 before realizing that was the max. It made progression feel like it stalled toward the end.

[b]Overall, I'd give Cyberpunk 2077 a 4.1/5 [/b]

So... Lemme break down something that happened... I accidentally ran a guy over because of the game's clunky vehicle controls. I get chased by the cops, and I am able to SOMEHOW trick the cops by hiding behind a dumpster. I accidentally ended up playing this game like a GTA game, and honestly?!! It's fun and addicting! This is a game that HOLDS your attention like an iron grip. There is a reason it's heralded as one of the best games of the early RTX era of PC gaming. The game is also drop dead GORGEOUS and still holds up today, almost 6 years later. Games don't NEED to look better than Cyberpunk 2077, if I am being completely honest. This is fine, as far as graphics go. There are SO MANY small little details that you can just miss if you're not intentionally looking around for them.

I can look around, not see something, see it again from the corner of my eye and go, "Hold on, is that a Kamen Rider reference?" (I haven't found said reference, but given the size of this game, and its numerous influences, it wouldn't surprise me to see said references)

Somewhere on Jig-Jig Street, some dude has some kind of magical girl anime sounding anime theme blasting on a boom box, and it's such an easy to miss detail. I caught it in the mid-afternoon, game time, and if I had waited around until evening, I probably would have missed it. Cyberpunk feels LIVED IN. You can see all kinds of shops, all kinds of bars, food stalls, etc, and there are so many people walking around. Many many people are just walking around in normal outfits, not really doing anything. But then you'll turn around and see a guy eating Chinese takeout. A lady at that same stall could then be arguing with the vendor at said stall, and if you have subtitles enabled, you'll see what they're arguing about.

Other times, you'll witness a lady punch a guy because he wouldn't leave her alone (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... I can't possibly relate to her at all... Le sigh...). Go to the pachinko parlor, and maybe you'll see a couple thugs walk in and start fist fighting each other. One time, I saw two guys shoot AND KILL each other!

Not to belabor all of the points I am making, I just wanna say that the atmosphere, the setting, etc all feel REAL! No wonder CD Projekt Red had a hard time getting this game working properly for two years or so... They put so much work and love into the setting, that honestly, to give the benefit of the doubt here, it's very easy to miss a lot of glitches and bugs. When you have a world so massive like Night City, yeah, a few bugs are going to slip through the cracks. 

So yeah... Honestly? My game of 2026. It's held my attention, and it's actually interesting.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 10/10 — I Have Become Cyberware
I bought Cyberpunk 2077 expecting a video game.

What I received was a life-altering neurological event.

I started playing at 8 PM. I looked away from the screen for what felt like five minutes.

It was 4:37 AM.

My character had committed approximately 17 felonies, acquired enough cyberware to qualify as industrial equipment, and somehow gotten emotionally attached to a man who was literally living inside my head.

The story had me laughing, crying, questioning capitalism, questioning my life choices, and staring silently at the ceiling at 3 AM wondering if Johnny Silverhand would respect me.

The city is gorgeous. The neon lights. The rain. The skyscrapers. The absolute criminal amount of atmosphere.

I walked into a nightclub and immediately forgot I was supposed to be doing the main quest.

I saw a random side mission.

I did the side mission.

The side mission had a deeper story than most movies.

Then I found another side mission.

Three hours later, I was halfway across Night City dressed like a radioactive disco cowboy carrying 14 guns I didn't need.

And the music?

DISGUSTINGLY GOOD.

Every time a song started playing, I suddenly felt like I had a tragic backstory and a motorcycle I was emotionally obligated to ride into the sunset.

This game has bugs, sure.

But honestly, I stopped seeing them as bugs.

They are features from the future.

My car flew into the sky? Cyberpunk.

An NPC stared directly into my soul? Cyberpunk.

Someone's arm became geometrically impossible? CYBERPUNK.

At some point I realized I wasn't playing Cyberpunk 2077 anymore.

Cyberpunk 2077 was playing me.

I have lost friends.

I have lost sleep.

I have lost all concept of responsible time management.

But I have gained something far more important:

A crippling emotional attachment to Night City.

Would recommend.

10/10.

My Cyberpunk 2077 Review.

SCORE SUMMARY:
• Story: 9/10
• Gameplay: 8/10
• Sidequests: 8.5/10
• Atmosphere: 9/10
• Soundtrack: 9/10
• Dlc: 10/10
OVERALL SCORE: 9

DETAILED COMMENTS:
• Story
 The story is great; we follow V, a mercenary trying to find his place in a city that wants to see everybody on the ground all the time. After stealing a chip from one of the world's largest corporations containing an engram of a terrorist who died decades ago, Johnny Silverhand, and to keep him stable, V finds himself in a race against time to find a way to remove this chip before Johnny's engram involuntarily takes possession of his body. As V faces this challenge, he interacts with various characters and becomes very close to Johnny, Panam, Judy, Kerry, and River, who are part of his journey in Night City. The game has multiple endings depending on your choices, and all of them are good and satisfying.
• Gameplay
 The gameplay is very satisfying; you can play in different ways. I initially played as a netrunner and found it quite fun, but I switched to a Sandevistan user with a katana and revolver. The game allows you to customize your cybernetic implants for different gameplay styles to suit each player's preference, and the game does a great job of this aspect of freedom. The character customization is very good; you can add various hairstyles, piercings, tattoos, clothes, etc. I only missed visible chrome effects, such as cybernetic arms and etc. It has a skill tree and item crafting. The only downside I felt was the vehicle mobility; the gameplay in vehicles is quite limited.
• Sidequests
  The game's side quests are mostly quite fun, such as the battles where you level up against characters we know from the story. My favorites were the ones with Jefferson Peralez and The Sinnerman. Some of them are really annoying, like the ones that report crimes all over the map.
• Atmosphere
 The atmosphere of this game is beautiful, however, it portrays late capitalism in an excellent way, where corporations don't see us as human beings, but as numbers that consume their products to generate profit. Night City is as dangerous as it is beautiful, a place full of neon billboards advertising capitalist companies that suck the life out of us, an oppressive city with everyone. The atmosphere captivates you in a surreal way, you really feel like an individual in a city that doesn't care about you; you see many people in vulnerable situations while others are rolling in money (this happens now, but in the game happens worst).
•Dlc
 One sin you absolutely CANNOT commit is not buying the Phantom Liberty expansion, it's one of the best expansions I've ever played in my life. The expansion takes us to a district inside Night City: Dogtown, a place dominated by former soldier Kurt Hansen who rules the place with an iron fist, We're going there to carry out a spy mission working together with the FIA, with the promise that we'll be able to get the Relic using Johnny's engram. In it, we meet incredible characters like the netrunner Songbird and Agent Reed. Where we have a story of espionage, betrayals, tears, and hope.

Night City is a colossal purgatory forged from steel and blood, a place where towering skyscrapers strangle the sun and neon light bleeds into the asphalt. This city never truly gives you a choice in how to live; it simply waits for you to decide how you will die. The cursed bullet we took to the head in that desolate landfill, thanks to Dexter DeShawn's betrayal, the very bullet Misty turned into a necklace, is not merely the beginning of the game. It is a ticking bomb hanging against our chest, the fatal price of our arrogance and our desperate hunger to become a legend. Every second that cold metal touches our skin, it whispers that we are slowly fading away.

The neon-drenched summits of Night City promise to carve your name into history in letters of gold, to make you an immortal legend. And at first, we believed that captivating lie. That is, until we lost Jackie, bleeding out in our arms in the back of that bloodstained Delamain cab. Jackie wanted to become a legend in Night City. He wanted his name to be remembered, to become someone who truly mattered. But as his blood slipped through our fingers, something inside V began to change for the very first time. In that backseat, V realizes that the pursuit of becoming a legend can actually mean burying the people you love with your own hands. The devastating loss of Jackie, followed by betrayal and the bullet she took to the head in that dark landfill, tears away the illusion Night City had built around her. V now knows that her time is slowly and irreversibly running out. And that realization becomes the first step in a long journey that slowly changes her ambition and the way she sees life and what truly matters.

The other paths the game offers confront you with the cost of becoming a legend. Trust Arasaka and you find yourself locked inside that orbital clinic, separated from your identity, your life, and the things that made you who you were, until you become little more than a corporate experiment. Even when you conquer everything in The Sun ending, reach the summit of Night City and touch the sun, you can still end up completely alone in the freezing void of space. The summit becomes the city's most magnificent, yet coldest, graveyard. And then, as the credits roll, the holo calls from your friends begin to play. Judy's tearful voice, Panam's fierce and desperate tone... They all point toward the same truth: the legacy you leave behind is not a soulless name carved into neon, but the lives you touched and the people who miss you when you are gone.

And this is exactly where Cyberpunk 2077's 5th Anniversary “City of Legends” trailer places V's entire journey before us, almost like pieces of the same realization. The lines in the trailer don't feel like random quotes. Together, they form a chain that gradually leads V toward questioning what truly matters after everything she has been through in Night City.

First comes the question: “If you could go back to the beginning, what would you try to change?” This question does not simply ask V to reconsider the things she has done. It makes her look back at the people she lost, the choices she made, and what remains after the entire journey. V is no longer the person she was at the beginning. At first, what mattered was rising through Night City, taking bigger jobs, and eventually becoming a legend everyone would know. But as time passes, the things that matter to V begin to change. Family, friendship, the people who stayed, and the people she truly loves begin to carry far more weight than the fame Night City promises.

Then the trailer continues: “You don't fight to win, or even stay alive...” This line shows that V's struggle has become something much larger than a simple fight for survival. Throughout her journey, the people she loses and the bonds she creates teach her that simply staying alive is not enough. A person isn't necessarily truly living just because they are still breathing. The real question is what that life is being lived for, and who you want beside you while you're living it.

Then comes that crucial line: “You might just make it to the major leagues...” At first glance, it sounds like the old Night City dream again, the dream of rising higher and becoming someone important. But within the flow of the trailer, the meaning shifts. It is no longer simply about reaching the top of Night City. What V ultimately reaches for is the feeling of belonging among the people who truly matter to her. The “major leagues” no longer feel like nothing more than the status Night City promised her. They become something closer to reaching a place where she can stand alongside the people she genuinely considers her family. The idea moves away from the city's command to “become a legend” and toward the much more personal question of “who are you with?”

And immediately after that comes the short but incredibly heavy line: “And just for a moment...” This is where the emotional weight of the entire trailer seems to condense into a few words. V is no longer seeking a name that will live forever. She wants to feel, even if only for a brief moment, that she truly matters to the people she loves. That brief moment becomes worth more than every neon light in Night City.

Finally comes the emotional peak: “Be something that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mattered.” To matter here is not about proving yourself to Night City or making sure everyone knows your name. What V ultimately wants is to mean something to the people she considers her family. To matter to the people who would fight for her, bleed beside her, and refuse to let her disappear without a fight. The point is no longer to be remembered as a legend. It is to have been genuinely loved and valued by the people who truly knew you.

This is where the deeper meaning of the “Never Fade Away” spirit becomes clear. True immortality is not becoming a chrome-plated god or the greatest legend Night City has ever known. It is being remembered by the people whose lives you touched. It is having people who would stand beside you when everything falls apart. And this is where V's journey truly changes. She stops searching for the value that Night City assigns to her and begins deciding what her own life is worth.

That is precisely why, at the border where the city's counterfeit lights finally disappear, The Star ending becomes more than an escape. It becomes V's strongest answer to everything Night City represents. Far away from the noise of corporate wars and neon streets, nothing can replace a nomadic family gathered around a campfire, the friendship of Panam and Mitch, or the simple tenderness of holding Judy's hand. As V feels the desert wind against her face atop the Panzer, she is finally taking her own fate back into her hands.

And that is why tearing the cursed bullet necklace from her throat and giving it to the wind carries so much weight. The exact moment that necklace disappears into the dust is the moment V leaves the myth of becoming a legend behind. She is no longer choosing the life Night City has designed for her. She is choosing her own life. Perhaps she only has six months left in that failing body. Perhaps the future remains uncertain. But breathing freely under the open sky, beside the people she loves and on her own terms, is worth more than an eternity of fame.

Because Cyberpunk 2077 was never truly about becoming the greatest legend Night City had ever seen. It was about discovering, in a city that teaches you to sacrifice everything for a name, what is truly worth holding on to. In the end, it is about choosing a life of your own, standing beside the people you love, and holding on to the hope that tomorrow might still bring something worth fighting for, no matter how much time you have left.

There is a hole the size of Antarctica in my heart after "completing" Cyberpunk 2077.

You'll not find anything different from many reviewers who have already praised the game. The graphics are great, gameplay is awesome, music hits differently, world-building is fantastic, characters are deeper than the Mariana Trench, and the story is great except for the endings, which all of them sucks from my point of view.

The reason is that the open world that is designed here is one of the best open worlds in any video game ever. This is one of the rarest games where I have rarely used fast travel! The vibe is unmatched compared to any other game. The world is not too big but detailed, contained, and content-rich; there are ubish! t-esqe icons, but those also have a little story and lore, so it was almost worth completing them!

Open world activities work here because each one connects to the greater lore of not only Night City but the entire world at that time. Every gig, every random encounter, every shard you pick up feels like it belongs to the same living, breathing, rotting city. Night City itself becomes a character — loud, beautiful, cruel, and addictive. You start treating the streets like home instead of a checklist.

Keanu Reeves, aka John Wick, aka Johnny Silverhand, is fabulous! This is again one of the rare instances where a celebrity was used properly, and he gave his 100% to create one of the most memorable characters in video games! The banter, the rage, the quiet moments… he just works. And the rest of the cast (Panam, Judy, River, Kerry, even the random fixers) all feel like real people stuck in the same neon meat-grinder.

Now that I have completed all endings, I'm half-broken. Half because Phantom Liberty is still ongoing (Idris Alba is also utilized amazingly, but that part comes in the Phantom Liberty review).

Endings, all of them sucks. I'm a sucker for happy endings, and here, we have zero. None of them provides our character with the solution that was required, and I'm pissed & sad.

But my V will keep fighting.

This game for me, really scratches an itch. For the longest time, I couldn't identify exactly what that itch was. As of writing this review, I think that I have come to a conclusion on what this game does for me. Cyberpunk 2077 does something that most other games do not and that is the blend of fiction with reality. Now I know what your're thinking: "What the hell are you talking about? Nothing in this game is real, are you boofing crack?" To the latter, you'd be correct. To the former, we have to look at Cyberpunk from its core premise. On its surface we can see that large corporate organizations essentially control the modern day world and that ordinary citizens struggle to survive on a daily basis. Very high tech and low life. That's not dissimilar from the world we live in today. We have large corporations that lobby and influence greatly the world that we live in and while many of us aren't mercs, we certainly have a lot of dead end jobs that require small gig jobs here and there to help make ends meet. While we don't have Mr. Studds and Braindances, we have smart TVs and smartphones. While the actual content of the game is science fiction, the principle of the game is very lifelike. There is no free lunch IRL and in Cyberpunk. This is the core of what I like so much about this game.

From a gameplay perspective, Cyberpunk has a whole hell of a lot to do and it is very replayable for me. You can play the game very differently each time you restart the story. From the lifepaths, the weapons and the skills, it can often feel like several games in one. My two favorite ways to play is with Sandevistan and bladed weapons or  Cyberdeck with ranged weapons. 

As far as graphical fidelity and artsyle is concerned, Pretty A+ in my book. I love the neon soaked night time in the city, the super clean militaristic areas and the worn down grunge impoverished areas, This game as lots of contrast that feels amazing and helps the stoytelling. My only complaints right now are the draw distance and textures popping in and out, which I postulate may be a problem with the game engine and not necessarily an issue with my hardware. 

The sound design is pretty good as well. I love the way the weapons sound, the way the cars rev up, and the different sound effects for performing certain actions like uploading quickhacks or activating the sandevistan. The music in the world and on the radio stations really adds depth to the world and fleshes it out. Also, the minor npcs sound funny as hell when you scare them. 

In conclusion, this game is about as much fun as you can have outside of the bedroom, unless you take your bedroom activites outside. At any rate, I'm clinically addicted to this game. Playing Cyberpunk is about as close as I can get to the feeling of the first time I tried heroin. Close enough.

I sometimes saw the saying online for other games that "the devs made such a pretty world and filled it with absolutely nothing interesting." Cyberpunk 2077 is a case study on how to avoid that.

Back in 2018, I visited gamescom in Köln for a narrated "first look" at a level that I am now pretty sure was within Pacifica. Some guy was sitting in the middle of this giant box, playing this level early and what I got to see there completely differs from what I played roughly 8 years later. This gameplay loop was not some sort of clever multiple choice do what you ever want bullcrap. This was run of the mill, Ubislop overworld faire gameplay, the equivalent of getting fast food for gaming. This is completely fine in theory, but we were sold anything but. And now, having actually played through Cyberpunk 2077...?

It's good. Great, even! I found V's female character to be my most favourite part of this entire trip, and all of the side content make such a good job at making me care about Panam, Misty, Viktor, Judy, Rogue, hell even Johnny. It took a bit to set in but I was really wanting to see it through the end.
With the gameplay loop being the usual open world explore -> loot -> sell -> repeat with stronger gear acquisition being a favourite in these games, I had a good time exploring Night City (looks absolutely stunning by the way) and seeing what's happening.

However, marketing sold us on so much more, and so I leave Night City after 40 hours with a bitter aftertaste, and a feeling of shame that marketing hyped this up so much to the point of setting unrealistic expectations for the playerbase. It makes me feel that CD Projekt Red, or at least part of the studio, has no faith in their own games staying power as art, they really should though. Because with Cyberpunk 2077, they've shown they are capable of offering incredibly realised beautiful worlds, and very strong narrative beats to support it that elevate the fictional Night City into something I won't forget about that easily.
