I had never written a game review before because I thought it was unnecessary. However, after playing Cyberpunk 2077, I felt a huge desire to share my thoughts. Honestly, I still find it hard to find the right words to describe everything I felt while playing.

At first, my expectations were around 7/10. I have always liked cyberpunk and dystopian worlds, so the concept immediately interested me. I had also heard that Cyberpunk 2077 was unfinished, full of problems, and far from a masterpiece. Still, I hoped I would like it.

But after a few hours, I realized that I was going to love this game.

Cyberpunk 2077 captivated me with its atmosphere, story, characters, gameplay, huge world and, especially, its music. The more I played, the more I realized that it wasn't just another open-world game. It was a world I wanted to stay in.

[h1] Story [/h1]

The story of Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best I have ever experienced in a game. From the very beginning, it was hard to imagine where it would lead and what would happen next.

The game stays with you even after you finish it. You keep thinking about what happened, the characters, their decisions, and the choices you made.

Cyberpunk 2077 explores many important topics: life and death, friendship, loss, loneliness, memory, the fear of being forgotten, and what it means to be yourself.

The idea of fighting for your own life isn't new, but the way CD Projekt Red used it is incredible. [spoiler] You literally end up with a person in your head who was once your enemy and the biggest threat to your life. However, they gradually become your friend and even try to save you.

The relationship between V and Johnny is one of the emotional cores of the game. Their relationship changes from hate and mutual distrust to real friendship. [/spoiler]

The side quests also feel meaningful. Many tell their own stories, develop the characters and world, and sometimes even add to the main story. Because of this, Night City gradually starts to feel alive.

[h1] Night City [/h1]

Night City is another reason to love this game.

At first, it seems incredible: neon signs, skyscrapers, implants, cars, advertisements, technology, gangs and corporations. You look at it and think, "This is the future".

But behind the neon signs are poverty, violence, addiction, exploitation and people simply trying to survive.

This contrast makes the atmosphere so strong. Even in a world where people can change almost any part of their bodies, human problems remain. People still fall in love, lose loved ones, fear death, feel lonely and search for the meaning of life.

[h1] Phantom Liberty [/h1]

[spoiler] It is worth mentioning Phantom Liberty. In my opinion, it is even stronger than the main story.

Song So Mi, or Songbird, and Reed are, for me, two sides of the same coin. Songbird tries to survive at any cost, just like V. Reed wants to save her, but he is also controlled by the president and the system he serves.

The best thing is that you can understand both of them. There is no simple "right" choice. Everyone has their own reasons, fears and beliefs.

That is why I found the main choice in Phantom Liberty so difficult.

The DLC's main musical theme makes the ending even more powerful. There is no simple answer where everyone ends up happy, and that leaves you with a very heavy feeling. [/spoiler]

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

The gameplay offers a lot of variety. You can play as a pure netrunner, a stealth character with silenced weapons, a monowire fighter, or use smart guns from behind cover.

And that's just one example.

I like that the game lets you create your own playstyle. Your V can be a netrunner, stealth killer, katana fighter, gunslinger, or someone who simply rushes into a room with a shotgun. Most importantly, these styles really feel different.

[h1] Music [/h1]

The soundtrack is truly incredible.

The tracks fit the situations perfectly and make you feel even more immersed in the world. Cyberpunk 2077 combines many styles, from loud and energetic tracks to slow, melancholic and tense ones.

Energetic music makes you feel like a cool mercenary with cyberimplants who can do almost anything. But when something quiet and melancholic starts playing, you see another side of this world. Behind the neon signs is a harsh reality, and V becomes an ordinary person who fears death, experiences loss, falls in love and searches for the meaning of life.

Each track creates its own mood or captures a particular situation.

When I listen to this music, the whole atmosphere of the game comes back. That's why I added almost every track to my playlist, and I still listen to them regularly.

It would be an insult to the composers not to add the Cyberpunk 2077 soundtrack to my playlist.

The only thing I regret is that some tracks were never released on digital platforms and remained available only in the game.

[h1] Flaws [/h1]

Of course, Cyberpunk 2077 isn't perfect.

The biggest problem becomes noticeable when trying to complete the game 100%. At first, additional activities help you explore Night City, but many eventually become repetitive. Gigs and interesting side quests are great, but some smaller activities turn into simply "clearing" areas.

There is also a contrast between how alive Night City seems and how much you can actually interact with it. The city is incredibly detailed, but outside quests, many NPCs and elements are mostly decoration. I wish there were more ways to simply live in this world.

Some characters could also have been developed further. Some left a strong impression on me, while others appeared, played their role and disappeared quickly. This is especially noticeable in Phantom Liberty, where the characters receive much more attention.

[spoiler] There is also a problem with the sense of urgency. The game constantly reminds you that V has limited time and needs to save their life quickly. At the same time, nothing stops you from putting this problem off for dozens of hours, driving around the city, completing gigs, buying cars and doing whatever you want. From a gameplay perspective, this is understandable, but sometimes it contradicts the story. [/spoiler]

However, these flaws are minor for me. When I think about Cyberpunk 2077, I don't remember repetitive activities or imperfect AI. I remember Johnny, Panam, Judy, Song So Mi, Reed, Night City, the music, my decisions, and the emotions the game made me feel.

[h1] Afterthoughts [/h1]

After about 20 hours, I realized that simply finishing the main story wouldn't be enough. I wanted to complete the game 100%.

I rarely want to explore all of a game's content, but in Cyberpunk 2077 I wanted to do everything: complete side quests, experience characters' stories, try different builds, make different choices, and explore Night City.

Even after finishing the game, you are left with the feeling that you have just stepped out of another life. That's why it was so hard to close the game and move on to something else.

[h1] Finally [/h1]

Even on my not very powerful laptop, I was able to fully enjoy this game. I especially appreciate the developers for making such a huge and beautiful world accessible even on relatively weak hardware.

Cyberpunk 2077 is the kind of game that makes it difficult to immediately start something new.

Maybe I couldn't describe everything I wanted to. Maybe some things are simply impossible to describe properly in words. However, I know one thing for sure:

Cyberpunk 2077 is a game I won't forget for a very long time.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games that completely sucked me into its world. Night City is easily one of the most impressive open-worlds I've explored. Everywhere you go there are huge buildings, neon lights, busy streets, advertisements and random events happening around you. The gameplay is really enjoyable too. You can choose how you want to play, whether that's running in with weapons, using stealth, hacking enemies or mixing everything together. The cyberware system also lets you customise V and create some pretty powerful builds.

The game does have some downsides. Night City can sometimes feel like there's more going on visually than there is to actually interact with, and some activities can become repetitive after a while. There are also moments where the open-world mechanics don't feel quite as deep as they could be.

Despite that, Cyberpunk 2077 is an incredible experience. The atmosphere, music, characters and story make it very easy to get lost in Night City.

This game finally clicked with me when it ended, and so I was yea, really glad that I finished it.

Tips: do not try to be a completionist like I did - do what makes sense for your character. ROLE PLAY. And don't forget to take it all in: the ambient dialogue, the news, the visuals, the framing of every scene in every mission. This is game that oozes style and atmosphere. It is not a choice between style and substance, it is a vibe that reaches out and throttles the player. I played this game on both the big screen and the small, and it never failed to fully immerse me in the depressive yet smouldering world of Night City. In my 100+ hours spent in the game I never once fast travelled, in fact it never crossed my mind to. Whilst the open world is not the most interactive, it is so full of details and charm that I can't help but notice things. And it is a kind of interactivity that engages the player's senses. There is just so much to SEE, so much to be AWARE OF. And so the imagination, like in any good RPG, ended up doing most of the world-building, making V, and the player, feel like just a small cog in a massive universe that stretches on and on. So yea, take your time with this game, read all the shards and codex entries, and it will reward you with a rare kind of immersion that you simply don't get in most open world games these days.

As for the story - without spoilers - hands down one of the best stories I have ever experienced? And I mean it: from the writing, to the presentation, down to the smallest details like the framing of the first-person camera angle. This game works on a moment-to-moment level, another instance where the themes of the story come to characterise the gamer's experience. In any other game this would have smacked of vanity, as when a film strings together powerful imageries that lack punch in the end due to a lack of cohesion. But Cyberpunk thrives on the ephemeral - vibes, passion, adrenaline - it works because it doesn't dwell on anything for too long. And whilst the text lacks the literary sophistication of the classics from which it draws - the game cannibalises its own script and creates/presents a story which fits the video game medium exceedingly well. I simply can't imagine reading or watching V's story - it has to be played, inhabited, lived in. Then the credits rolled and the post video game depression hit harder than ever.

Still experiencing heavy withdrawal and I'm not kidding.

The gameplay offers decent freedom. I am not going to pretend that it is the deepest game mechanically, or that it has the most thought-out levels. Cyberpunk has to trade breadth with depth, and this is the most apparent when it comes to the level design. The enemy placement and the infiltration is surprisingly amateurish given the masterful storytelling which has been on abundant display. You simply do not get multiple entry points, or synergetic gadget use which often come with these types of games. Rather, everything is stats based which means if you have not built a character a certain way, then you will HAVE TO approach any level a given way. Freedom only ever begins at the first gun shot. And so if you are the sneaky gamer who prefers to take enemies out one by one instead of going in guns blazing you will find that the gameplay stabilises into the same rhythm pretty quickly - ping to discover enemies, upgrade pistol to max, headshots everyone. The usual AAA fanfare. Sadly, the safest play is not often the most exciting. That said, if you have the intrinsic motivation to look cool, there is plenty of room to amp up the spectacle. Just don't expect the pieces to always work as expected. It is surprising, that given the budget that is clearly behind Cyberpunk, the game can feel quite janky at times. But nothing gamebreaking luckily, if you are playing this now in 2026.

This game will surprise you, awe you, and make you cry by the time you put it down. I thought I had fully burnt out on it but something kept me going. It is truly a visionary game which can feel slow and pedestrian at first. But stick with it, and it will reward you one of the most impactful stories ever told in video games.

The most immersive, fun game I've played in years. 

Someone I saw a review from described it as 'doing missions and then riding home with your buddies in the car after', and I'd agree with that general synopsis of the gameplay loop. 

It's funny that the ride after probably became my favourite part. The voice acting, the lines, the fact you can look out the car window at Night City rolling by while you think of your reply to a question... I've never played a more immersive RPG from a look and feel perspective. 

Yes, I am utterly blessed to have a high end PC. So that helps. But after playing some on Steam Deck, I'd say that even on lesser hardware the immersion from this game comes mostly from the atmosphere CDPR built so carefully and the characters that are really hard to pick from as you make your end game choices. If you're a Bladerunner / Altered Carbon sci-fi junky, the questions asked by this game of the human psyche are nothing short of riveting as you explore a world shattered by corruption and the evisceration of what it means to be human. 

Another thing - I think people don't like RPGs that 'end'. They want you to beat the final boss and then roam forever free with the god-killing character you've created. But to me, Cyber Punk having an 'ending' (I don't think that's a spoiler - the game has been out long enough) meant that I valued my last few hours with V all the more. I was more emotionally invested knowing I was reaching a conclusion. I think the last time I sat down to finish a game with this much anticipation was Bioshock: Infinite. 

I probably could have spent more time in this world, but these days with a job and responsibilities, 50hrs felt about right. It has only left me eager to replay it all again in a few months with the Phantom Liberty DLC this time around. 

Thanks for reading!

Cyberpunk 2077 is the only game where you can go from having a casual conversation with a vending machine to fist‑fighting a cyber‑enhanced gorilla man in a back alley, all before breakfast. It’s a neon‑soaked fever dream, a tech‑dystopia vacation package, and a glitchy circus that somehow became one of the best RPGs out there.

Night City: The World’s Most Dangerous All‑Inclusive Resort
Night City is gorgeous. It’s vibrant. It’s alive. It’s also trying to kill you every five minutes.

You’ll be walking down the street admiring the neon skyline and—boom—someone’s car explodes. Not because of crime. Not because of gang violence. Just because Night City is built like it was coded by interns on Red Bull.

And yet… you love it.
It’s like visiting Las Vegas if Vegas had cybernetic arms, megacorporations, and existential dread baked into the architecture.

The Story: Existential Crisis, But Make It Stylish
You play as V, a mercenary who accidentally installs a brain‑haunting rockstar terrorist into their skull. Johnny Silverhand is equal parts mentor, menace, and malfunctioning Alexa. He pops up to give advice, insult you, or remind you that you’re dying. Very supportive.

The story is legitimately fantastic—emotional, intense, and full of characters who feel real enough that you’ll miss them when they’re gone.
Even the side quests slap harder than a malfunctioning cyber‑arm.

Combat: Guns, Blades, Hacking, and Occasionally Throwing Furniture
Cyberpunk lets you fight however you want:

Sneak around like a cyber‑ninja

Hack people’s brains until they catch fire

Run in with a shotgun and zero life insurance

Punch enemies so hard they forget physics

It’s chaotic, stylish, and extremely satisfying—especially once you realize you can hack someone’s cyber‑legs so they forget how to stand.

The Glitches: Comedy Gold (Mostly Fixed, But Never Forgotten)
Cyberpunk launched with bugs so legendary they deserve their own museum wing. NPCs T‑posing in the street, cars spawning from the sky, and police teleporting behind you like cyber‑ninjas who skipped the tutorial.

Most of that’s fixed now, but the memories live on.
Cyberpunk’s glitches were the closest thing gaming had to slapstick comedy.

The City Feels Alive… Even When It’s Actively Trying to Mug You
Night City is packed with detail—ads, crowds, conversations, weird robots, questionable food vendors, and people who look like they haven’t slept since 2041. It’s immersive in a way few games manage.

You don’t just play Cyberpunk.
You exist in it.
You suffer in it.
You thrive in it.
You get run over by a taxi in it.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a chaotic masterpiece.  
It’s stylish, emotional, hilarious, occasionally broken, and absolutely unforgettable. It’s the kind of game where you finish a mission, stare at the skyline, and think, “Wow… I should probably go do another mission instead of fixing my real‑life problems.”

If you want a game that’s equal parts brilliance and absurdity, Cyberpunk 2077 delivers.

If you want a game that never glitches… well, Night City has a message for you:
“We don’t do that here.”

[h3] 9/12 Міцний норміс [/h3]

[h1]CDPR Redeemed[/h1]

[h2]The Hype Train[/h2]
As a major Witcher 3 fan, I was well and truly on the hype train prior to Cyberpunk's release. I remember when the first teaser for the game came out and getting increasingly excited with each subsequent trailer. Then, after multiple delays, the game finally came out, and you all know the rest.

I felt not just let down by CDPR, but also misled. Honestly, if it wasn't for Steam's refund policy, I would have said that releasing the game in that state was downright anti-consumer.

Like many others, I closed the game and only came back every six months or so to check up on it. Eventually, I stopped coming back altogether. By this point, CDPR was dead to me. I didn't intend to buy another game from them again.

[h2]The Redemption[/h2]
When Phantom Liberty released, every headline in my feed was saying Cyberpunk was fixed, so reluctantly, I reinstalled the game and decided to give it one more try.

For once, the internet did not lie.

The game is fixed. It's exactly what it should have been in 2020. I'm still not happy about how everything went down, but I have to hand it to them. CDPR could have cut and run, but they didn't. They produced exactly what they promised, just three years later than they should have.

[h2]Gameplay Loop[/h2]
It's a big ♥♥♥♥-off RPG with futuristic guns, swords, and ♥♥♥♥. It's all tied together with that excellent CDPR writing and outstanding visuals.

Not much more I can say than that. Everything about this game has already been said.

[h2]Stutter Struggle?[/h2]
Nope. In fact, it has some of the best CPU multicore scaling I've come across.

It will utilise your whole CPU, which helps prevent you from getting bogged down by the same sort of CPU, shader, and traversal stutter that plagues so many games today.

The one thing I would say is that, as much as you'll be tempted to crank the visuals and turn on all the fancy ray-tracing settings, the game still looks great at Medium. The extra smoothness just makes the gunplay feel that much better.

I do know that the game received a lot of criticism for a widespread of bugs and such on release. However, as someone who played the game for the first time just recently and just completed it, I can say that I found it amazing.

I'm a big fan of The Witcher series so I did have quite high expectations and honestly, I believe they were met well. I'm not gonna say that the game is completely free from bugs and issues even now because it's not but I can say that I thoroughly enjoyed playing it.

The main storyline and, I'll call them "main side quests", are very well-made, intriguing, enjoyable and not to forget, emotional. The reason I call them main side quests are because there are a few side quests that aren't necessarily needed to finish the game but are deeply relevant to the story and missing out on them effectively means you are missing out on big parts of the story. As far as stories go, I would say that Cyberpunk was something I wouldn't want to miss out on. As a completionist I could also add that the side content other than the "main side quests" quickly grow boring and is a bit too much, such as the NCPD Scanner Hustles and gigs which are MANY and aren't especially fun or interesting after you've done a few.

Gameplay-wise, I think the combat varies from effortless to slightly difficult. I played the game on normal difficulty and only ever thought the enemies posed a threat at early levels but as soon as you started getting better gear and improved your build, it almost became too simple. The combat is still fun and since you can play stealthy, straight-forward combat or with quickhacks as a netrunner you have a few choices on how you approach combat in this game. I also really enjoyed exploring the open world with a series of different vehicles at my disposal, except when my car broke down for unkown reasons... (you'll know it when it happens).

I do want to mention the customization opportunities, where you can create and customize your character however you like aswell as use fancy clothes and all but the reason why I'm bringing this up is actually because I find it useless. You will barely see your character at all throughout your gameplay (except for a few specific situations) which makes the customization kind of pointless in my opinion. The only thing that really matters is whether your character is male or female for some interactions with certain characters.

As a separate part here, I'll mention the DLC, PL (Phantom Liberty). I very much enjoyed it and it feels like the developers put more time into the side content here because most gigs in Dogtown actually has more of a "story" and isn't just the same thing over and over. The main story line in PL is also very fun and comes with a handful of difficult decisions. Trust me when I say that you'll have a hard time choosing the "right" decision in this DLC.

To summarize, I really enjoyed Cyberpunk 2077 even if it is somewhat expensive. I would still say it is worth the price especially since you can sink a lot of hours into it. 

I hope this review helped you decide if this is a game for you or if you'd rather keep looking. Good luck and have fun gaming!

[h1]The Gist[/h1]
When I played Cyberpunk 2077 at launch, I thought it was little more than a decent game held up by phenomenal writing. Years later, I decided to start over and ended up playing one of my favorite games of all time. 

[h1]What I Liked[/h1]
✪ Superb writing and ability to tell stories remains unchanged since release. However, thanks to the plethora of bug fixes that have gone on since, the world is much more immersive. Not having so many visually jarring glitches, bugs that interfere with progression and obnoxious crashes made me appreciate the game’s masterfully written tales even more than I did before.

✪ Before I switch gears from the writing, Cyberpunk 2077 takes place in a dark, depressing and mean-spirited setting that stays true to its core for the entire ride. It’s one of the only games I’ve ever played that genuinely makes me feel bad—like, little aches from emotional damage, bad—and that’s so damn good. Too many games these days strive to be happy tales with good endings that always give the protagonist a hero’s welcome and saint’s end. 

✪ CDPR once again does an excellent job with world design. Night City is gorgeous in a twisted kind of “I’d never want to live here, or even visit, but I see the appeal” kind of way. I seldom explored areas that felt like copies of another, encouraging me to explore everything I could. NPCs would often be closely examined to get a look at their models and attire, with extra bits like the game’s ads and short animations being just as carefully crafted as the world they reside in.  

✪ With over 300 hours of playtime, the mechanics, build variety and immense amount of ways to approach different situations still feel a bit overwhelming, in a good way. This is mostly due to the fact that, without mods, no V can acquire everything the game has to offer at once. Traditional perks are unlocked by skill points acquired by leveling, and permanent passive buffs unlock as you complete certain actions. However, there are also a lot of cybernetic enhancements and hacks to choose from, and a limited number of spots to work with.

✪ There is a whole lot to do with a decent amount of variety, even among quests that are the same type. Even now, I distinctly remember seeing characters and quests online that I haven’t discovered myself, despite getting all of the achievements.

✪ Cyberpunk 2077 is mostly a game that follows the “style over stats” approach for attire. The pieces of equipment that actually do have stats can be equipped, then overlayed with a transmog system called Wardrobe, which lets you save different outfits that you can change into almost anytime. Even better is the fact that you don’t need to keep the clothes you want to wear in your inventory. Once you pick up a piece of clothing, it gets registered to your wardrobe right away so you can scrap or sell it to free up space. Keep the stuff with stats you like, though.

✪ Photo Mode is unfortunately underwhelming in most titles, but Cyberpunk 2077 has the best so far; at least natively. The simplified complexity of its settings allow for folks of all levels of creativity to put together some incredible shots. Being able to spawn your favorite NPC’s, make them pose, adjust their expressions for immersion’s sake and so much more is great, too. 

✪ REDmod makes this game one of the easiest to mod and maintain, regardless of what mod manager you use. I’m someone who changes their mind a lot when it comes to mods and has a tendency to uninstall some mods while introducing new ones in the middle of long playthroughs. I had no issues with that, here.

[h1]What I Didn't Like[/h1]
✘ The game’s been out for 6 years at the time of writing, and despite everything else they’ve added to the game, a flashlight wasn’t one of them. I remember complaining about how dark some of the areas were before I switched to an OLED monitor. Now, I wouldn’t be able to see a thing without this mod: [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/cyberpunk2077/mods/27721] Much Better Flashlight[/url].

[h1]Nitpicks[/h1]
• Just about every weapon you get as a quest reward from a major NPC is a pistol or revolver. I understand that it’s the most practical pair of weapons, but some variety would have been nice.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Cyberpunk 2077 started off in pretty rough shape, but it still managed to be a good game despite that. Now it’s a must-play that deserves a seat at the table with gaming’s other masterpieces. I really hope we get a surprise expansion before Cyberpunk 2, just like we’re getting with The Witcher 3.

Cyberpunk 2077 started with a pretty bad launch. There were bugs, performance problems, missing features and a lot of things that clearly weren't ready. Even now, some bugs still exist, but after finally playing through the game and Phantom Liberty, I can honestly say that underneath all of that is one of the best RPG experiences I've had.

Night City is incredible. The atmosphere, music, characters, quests and the sheer amount of things you can discover made me want to keep exploring even when I wasn't following the main story. The combat and build variety are also fantastic, and I loved being able to shape my male V into the kind of character I wanted.

But the characters are what really made this game memorable for me.

Johnny Silverhand is easily one of those gaming characters I don't think I'll ever forget. Keanu Reeves absolutely put his own personality into the role, and Johnny never felt like just another NPC following me around. I didn't always agree with him and I definitely wouldn't call him a great guy, but that's exactly what made his character interesting. Saying goodbye to Johnny when I chose the Star ending was genuinely sad.

And speaking of the Star ending, I went with Panam and the Aldecaldos. Out of all the choices I had, that was the ending I wanted for my male V. It was emotional and bittersweet, but it felt right. After everything V goes through, having people who are actually willing to stand beside him and leave Night City together gave the ending a feeling of hope that I really appreciated.

Saul's death hit me harder than I expected too. Saul was a great character, and losing him genuinely hurt. I still miss the guy.

Phantom Liberty was another highlight. Dogtown felt completely different from the rest of Night City, and the expansion brought a much more focused and darker story. Solomon Reed was interesting, but personally, I never really felt that Reed was a great guy. I chose not to kill him, but I also didn't completely trust him.

Songbird was another difficult choice. I didn't want to side with her because I didn't feel that was the right thing to do, so I ultimately chose to disconnect her and free her from everything instead. Phantom Liberty constantly put me in situations where there wasn't an obvious good choice, and I loved that about it.

Judy and Panam also deserve a special mention because both of them became some of my favorite characters in the entire game. Judy's story had this emotional weight to it that I really wasn't expecting, especially seeing everything she goes through and how much she genuinely cares about the people around her. Her questline is one of those parts of Cyberpunk that sticks with you long after you're done with it.

And then there's Panam. Panam quickly became one of the characters I cared about the most. She's stubborn, reckless, aggressive and sometimes an absolute pain in the ass, but that's exactly what made her feel real. Her relationship with V develops naturally through the story, and the Aldecaldos genuinely felt like a family by the end. That's why choosing the Star ending with Panam felt so satisfying to me. After everything V had been through, leaving Night City with Panam and the Aldecaldos felt like the closest thing to a happy ending V could realistically get.

Judy and Panam aren't just romance options or side characters. They're two of the people who make V's journey feel personal, and I'm glad Cyberpunk gave them the amount of attention and development they deserved.

After finishing everything, what stands out to me isn't the bugs, the technical problems or even the insane amount of content. It's the characters. V, Johnny, Panam, Saul, Songbird, Reed and everyone else made Night City feel like a place I actually spent time in rather than just another open world.

Cyberpunk 2077 may have started badly, but what CD Projekt Red eventually turned it into is something special.

I came for Night City.

I stayed for the people.

And honestly, saying goodbye was harder than I expected.

Having just finished getting all achievements during my first playthrough of this game (and doing all the side quests, gigs, NCPD scanners, etc. that I had available to me), all I can say is that this might genuinely be one of the best games that I have ever played. For the longest time, I swore I would never play this game after I had heard how bad the launch was for it, with the game being unplayable for many people, even with decent computers. With that being said, after Edgerunners released, I heard people picked up the game again and I was hearing nothing but praise, especially following the 2.0 update they put out later on. I personally found the Edgerunners anime to be really awesome, and even recently did a rewatch of it since I had started playing the game. I'd say it was the anime, which was followed by people's good words towards it that made me rethink my outlook on this game, and lead me to give it a shot just recently when I was able to get both the game and DLC for cheap during the Steam Summer Sale.

With that being said, I want to get into what I loved about this game. For starters, the Night City seen in-game genuinely feels alive. It's almost ironic, a game where there are multiple sentient and conscious AIs that are capable of thinking for themselves somehow also manages to almost make you think the same about the people you interact with in the game. I myself found several different interactions just randomly, either from looking at a certain location for a couple seconds or by bringing up certain dialogue options. Additionally, the characters are all very well-written and do a phenomenal job of fleshing out the world just by existing. Characters like Jackie, Johnny, Panam, Judy, River, Rogue, and so many others do such a great job breathing life into this world through their questlines and interactions. It's clear that the game really wants you to become attached to these characters, and they want you to feel happy when they're happy or sad when they're sad.  I found myself on numerous occasions becoming attached to characters, especially the ones that I interacted with the most. And of course, if I'm talking about characters I cannot forget to bring up the most important one, V. V is such a great character, even though they are the player character. I personally chose to play as Male Streetkid V, and I found myself loving the way he interacted with those around him, especially his typical banter between him and Johnny. The freedom that this game gives you with the world, allowing you to go basically wherever you want and do almost anything you could want to do in Night City, really helps V feel like a real person. Additionally, the choice to also have Keanu Reeves be the depiction for Johnny was really good, and he played the role absolutely amazingly to the point where it might be my favorite role I've seen him do (For reference, I have watched the Matrix trilogy plus the new one, John Wick 1-4, and Speed). To tie it all up, these well-written characters were used in such a phenomenal story about struggle, with a desire to become something important and leave a mark on the world. The fact that this game also has multiple endings helps solidify the freedom it gives you, allowing you to side with several different people to tackle your problems based on choices you have made throughout the story. There is even a "secret" ending that I was unable to get since I failed to pick the correct dialogue options during a certain part of the story, but the fact that such an ending even exists is what makes this game so special.

To wrap this up, I also want to briefly discuss the DLC since I had played that as well, and to be blunt, it might be the best DLC I have played for any game ever (so far). I have played many DLCs for many games that add on to the original story in a meaningful manner, while also not feeling mandatory, and I consider those to be good DLCs. With that being said, I can almost not imagine playing Cyberpunk 2077 without the Phantom Liberty DLC because it alone is simply that good. The DLC is essentially a whole other main plotline, which even supplies the game with an additional ending upon the completion of the DLC (depending on choices made). The DLC unlocks access to an otherwise restricted part of Night City known as Dogtown and revolves around a situation that occurs there. The DLC on its own is decently long (I'd wager 15-30 hours depending on your method of interacting with it), and even has around 4 different ways that things can turn out. I found myself being constantly posed moral questions for which I had no answer to in this DLC, questions that felt like I would lose with either choice I make. I am not often mentally challenged by a game in such a way, so I often found myself sitting and thinking about what to do at these times. While the main game has some of these kinds of choices as well, I felt that it was much more difficult to discern the "correct" choice to make in the quests and gigs in the DLC. Phantom Liberty also introduces some amazing characters as well, such as Songbird and Solomon Reed (who is portrayed by Idris Elba) and once again they just improve this DLC so much. The conflicts, breakdowns, resolutions, and so much more that are posed in the main questline really make the characters feel human and make Night City seem so much more real.

Now to be clear, I won't say the game is without problems. I found there to still be some bugs here and there, plus I had my fair share of crashes or technical difficulties, but I think I can look past those. Overall, I truly had a one-of-a-kind experience playing Cyberpunk 2077 with the Phantom Liberty DLC, experiencing something that I don't think can be equally supplied by any other game. Because of this, I want to extend my deepest gratitude to CD Projekt Red and Mike Pondsmith (the creator of the tabletop game that this game is based on) for creating such a beautiful world for the people to immerse themselves in. Anyhow chooms, I thank you for reading my extremely long love-letter to this game, and I'll see you all for Cyberpunk 2.

Cyberpunk 2077 — A Game That Proved Redemption Is Possible

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best examples of a game that completely changed the way I look at developers and their commitment to their players.

When Cyberpunk 2077 launched, it was a disaster. It was buggy, unstable, poorly optimized, and nowhere near the experience that many players expected. CD Projekt Red deserved the criticism they received. They made enormous promises, and at launch, they failed to deliver on them.

But what happened afterward is what makes Cyberpunk 2077 special.

CD Projekt Red didn't simply move on. They kept working.

Year after year, they continued improving the game, fixing bugs, rebuilding systems, listening to criticism, and eventually delivering the massive Phantom Liberty expansion and the 2.0 update. They didn't just patch a few crashes and call it a day—they fundamentally improved the game.

And that is where Cyberpunk 2077 stands apart from many other games.

It demonstrates something that is becoming increasingly rare in the AAA industry: developers who genuinely care about making their game better after launch.

The irony is that Cyberpunk 2077's redemption makes Bethesda's approach increasingly difficult to defend.

Bethesda has built an entire identity around its games being ambitious, expansive, and sometimes buggy. And perhaps the most infamous phrase associated with the company is Todd Howard's "It just works."

The problem is that sometimes it clearly doesn't.

Bethesda's games have historically shipped with bugs, technical problems, dated systems, and questionable design decisions, yet there has often been an attitude of this is simply how Bethesda games are. Players are expected to accept the quirks because the games are huge and ambitious.

Cyberpunk 2077 initially fell into the same trap—but CD Projekt Red eventually chose a different path.

They essentially said:

"We screwed up. Now we're going to fix it."

And they actually did.

Today, Cyberpunk 2077 feels like a completely different game from the one that launched in 2020. The combat, police system, skill trees, vehicle gameplay, cyberware, AI, UI, progression, and countless other systems have been improved or rebuilt. Phantom Liberty demonstrated that CD Projekt Red wasn't interested in simply maintaining the status quo—they wanted to prove what the game could have been.

That's what I respect most.

Cyberpunk 2077 isn't impressive because it launched perfectly. It is impressive because the developers refused to let their failure define the game.

There is something admirable about seeing developers acknowledge their mistakes and spend years rebuilding the trust they lost.

Meanwhile, Bethesda's reputation increasingly feels like it relies on the same old formula: release an ambitious game, accept the bugs as part of the experience, and tell players that eventually everything will work.

"It just works."

Well, CD Projekt Red showed us something better:

"It didn't work. So we fixed it."

That's the difference between defending a product and being passionate about improving it.

Cyberpunk 2077 ultimately became more than just a great RPG. It became a lesson in accountability, perseverance, and what a developer can accomplish when it genuinely commits to its promises.

I won't forget how terrible the launch was.

But I also won't forget what CD Projekt Red did afterward.

[h1]Cyberpunk 2077[/h1] Is one of those games you can honestly call one of the best things you can experience in life. Not just a “good game”, but something that really sticks with you.

The gameplay is top-tier: shooting, progression, implants — everything works and feels satisfying. The locations are highly detailed, every district has its own vibe. Night City actually feels alive — not just a backdrop, but a real world you want to spend time in.

The characters are alive, charismatic, and memorable.

Also, the music is amazing and fits the atmosphere perfectly. I often caught myself just driving around the city listening to the tracks.

The game is packed with easter eggs, and it’s genuinely fun to find them. There are references to a lot of other games and pop culture: The Witcher, Fallout, Portal, Death Stranding, Dark Souls, Doom, GTA San Andreas, Half-Life, Contra, System Shock, and many more. There are also references to movies, anime, and even real people like Hideo Kojima. And a nice bonus — easter eggs related to Cyberpunk: Edgerunners, which is great if you’ve watched the anime.

There are also many different endings, which is a big plus. They’re all interesting and have their own tone — there’s no single “right” choice.

The DLC is fine, but I’m not a big fan. It’s not bad, but the main game hit way harder for me.

Where to start... This game confused me so much at first, but I have to say that it does a tremendous job with its well-written characters and immersive universe. The level design is simply breathtaking.

The only real issue I have with the game is its gameplay, which sometimes feels a bit too simple. The cyberware system also feels somewhat limited and not particularly innovative, in my opinion. That being said, the game does offer a wide variety of playstyles, such as stealth, close-range combat, Sandevistan builds, and so on. I might be biased, though, because FPS games are definitely not my favorite genre.

For me, Cyberpunk's greatest strength remains its storyline, which genuinely surprised me. I would probably consider it one of the best stories I've ever experienced in a video game. Night City captivates you in a strange way and can even change the way you think about certain things in life.

Most of the time, I never bother doing side quests in games, but I found Cyberpunk's side missions to be just as good as the main ones, with some of them being even better. Special mention goes to the Jefferson Peralez questline, which was definitely one of the most memorable for me.

Being immersed in this dystopian world, alongside all these different characters, made me reflect on several philosophical questions. One of the most memorable examples is Dex DeShawn's famous question about whether you'd rather live a quiet life or go out in a blaze of glory.

I also love the way CD Projekt RED undermines the traditional idea of stories leading toward a happy ending. Here, instead, we are caught in an endless cycle that will never truly end as long as Night City remains standing. People come and go, legends are born and die, but the city survives and preserving  them as they should be : legends.

I have now played this game for about a day, after buying it on sale over 5 years after its initial release date. I personally think this game would've probably been worth full price, but I love a good sale me so that certainly tipped the scales. I was concerned about the hardware requirements, especially after everything people were saying upon release. Overall, my machine is a solid gaming laptop, slightly below recommended specs but could run it fine overall with solid but not the best graphics. This was completely fine for me, I was still impressed with the detail and this did not affect my immersion into the game at all. On to the main aspects of the game itself:

This first thing is the immersion, the movement feels crisp, the environment is detailed, and the game gives you a lot of agency. When you play this game you feel like you are in a dystopian city in the distant but not-too-distant future. I think that's the main selling point of this game, how well it manages to immerse you into another world. I would say that they should have set it a bit further in the future though, particularly the flashbacks to 2023 where technology and politics were already shown to be far more advanced/different from the present day. 

The combat mechanics were fun and stylistically varied, although I'd say the enemies took a while to die which led to ammo consumption problems for automatic weapons. This is the case even on lower difficulties, and even if the battles themselves are not too difficult.

[Spoilers] The storyline is solid, and engaging, you follow your character from a lowly hoodlum into a competent but not omnipotent mercenary for hire. You feel for the characters you meet on the way, each has a distinct and interesting personality and its great to interact with them, you have so many options to do this. However, the endings fell a bit flat for me. Even the best ending is kind of bittersweet, in the sense that your character is stuck withering away. I'm not necessarily against bad/sad endings, but I think either triumphant victory or last-stand/blaze-of-glory death options would've also been good here. Maybe that's just me though, some people say it's the storytelling element but current options feel narratively restrictive to me after everything your character has gone through. 

The level of content for a single-player game is outstanding, the level of interaction with characters and the detail in the environment as discussed, but also the amount of quests and missions, the character customisation options, weapons and upgrades, houses, cars, radio stations etc. I still have a lot of things to do even after over 24h of playtime. 

Overall probably a 9/10. Definitely one of the better games I've ever played.

[h1]A City Worth Burning For[/h1]

Background: I played this game to completion on launch when it was a mess (or at least within its first 6 months of release) and returned to do another 100% run with Phantom Liberty now. What CDPR have managed to achieve by slowly revamping this game is nothing short of incredible. 

[h2]Graphics[/h2]

The graphical fidelity of this game is well documented so I won't spend too much time here, but the game is gorgeous - the part I find [b]really[/b] impressive graphically is how rich and dense the environment is. Unless you're actively looking for it by going to the edge of places you're not really supposed to be (or you experience a glitch here or there - and you will!) - you're unlikely to come across even so much as an ugly texture in this game. It also all feels very cohesive. Just make sure you calibrate your brightness settings - particularly gamma if you've got an HDR screen.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

Do you like Deus Ex Human Revolution/ Mankind Divided? If so, this game has that on crack. As well as a lot more for you to dig your teeth into. I thoroughly enjoyed my recent return to NC - I ran a stealth/ netrunner/ melee build and had so much fun running around the city, "ghost"ing missions and taking out hoards of "gangoons" without anyone knowing what had happened. The game also has many options for pure action if that's your thing.

Getting from place to place is a pleasure, particularly when you've unlocked some movement speed upgrades and - I cannot recommend this enough - get the double jump leg implants as soon as you can. They improve the walking traversal so so much. I also enjoyed using motorbikes almost exclusively during this run, they're a lot easier to navigate with. The driving in general I think has been improved, or at least that's what it felt like. I found myself frequently choosing to drive from place to place to take in the sights rather than making use of the fast travel.

This is a personal nitpick, but I loathe sandbox games that don't allow you to fast travel from the map. Having to walk to a fast travel point to fast travel to another point feels dumb, but many games have this design decision for one reason or another. I just find it really annoying not being able to click on a map point and teleport to it when so many other games do this.

[h2]Music[/h2]

Fantastic, particularly in the Phantom Liberty expansion. The game is full of bangers that absolutely fit the style and tone of the "era" and the vibe of Night City - I can't fault it. I do wish there was a little more variation in the radio stations - there are lots of them, but the genre doesn't seem to shift too much between them.

[h2]Story[/h2]

I'd probably rate the story as excellent, or at least very [i]very[/i] good. Like any game with mass amounts of content and an open environment, it's easy to introduce your own pacing issues depending on your approach to side content. The magical thing about this game's side content is that so much of it is rich and steeped in impressive variability. You can do one random Gig for a fixer and become immersed in the story of that single situation by reading emails, overhearing conversations while you're infiltrating an area, or just speaking to the characters.

The main plot I liked - I won't go into detail to avoid spoilers, but I found it thought provoking, touching at times, ridiculous (in a good way) at others, and even disturbing. That's kind of the point.

I mentioned variability in the side content, but that variation in the scenes/ lines/ reactions in main story missions is honestly extremely impressive. I'm a big fan of RPG's with choices and consequences, and it definitely does this aspect very well. I just finished up achievement hunting which required the different endings - and the variability not just in the endings themselves, but the missions leading up to those, was an insane surprise.

[h2]Stability[/h2]

In spite of the game being in an exponentially better state than it was when it initially released, I still encountered somewhat frequent crashes and bugs. Sometimes these were graphical - a texture shooting to the moon (massive triangles), the ocean straight up not loading - sometimes these were progression related (example: I couldn't interact with an object to progress a quest, but saving/ reloading on the spot fixed it). 

The worst offender is probably the random crashing though. I'd turn a corner on the way to a mission and it would just freeze up and crash out of the game completely, resulting in me troubleshooting quite a few times. I'd reload the game, restart my PC, change settings, and sometimes it'd be fine, others it wouldn't. It sucks, but the game is absolutely worth persevering with.

Excellent game. I feel like now CDPR have mastered this game, I really do hope they make a sequel in future. I'll wait to see how stable it is before buying though!

Cyberpunk 2077 is a fascinating case to me.

Few games have launched to such disastrously disappointing results -- at least proportionate to their hype at the time. And I do mean *at the time.*

The catastrophic launch of the game wasn't actually the fault of CDPR's development team, but rather upper management and board of directors; and they promised *alot* that the devs could not realistically expect to fulfill. I won't get too into the details, because this is a rather famous case and people far more knowledgeable on the topic could summarize it better than me, but essentially promises were made that were pretty much actually impossible to pull off with modern technology, like having an *entire, real life city's* worth of individualized NPCs down to each having their own names, jobs and schedules. Which is an utterly ridiculous proposition of course, but people will take your promises for the game at face value. And they did. Obviously this was not possible and was not delivered; as was the case with many of the false promises made by the parties responsible within the company. On top of that, even without making such absurd promises the game was rushed incredibly hard by these same parties; over and over again they had given unrealistic promises on the release date for the game as well, and it resulted in the dev team continuously having to delay the game to give it the development time it truly needed. On launch, the game was absolutely riddled with game-breaking bugs, janky, inconsistent and punishing physics, visual glitches, and development oversights.

Now, by this point if you really are unfamiliar with the game's current state, you might be wondering why this review recommends the game. And well, in short, I feel like CDPR's development team has done an excellent job salvaging a historically disastrous release, and has transformed it into one of the best action RPG's you can get nowadays, especially if you value writing, worldbuilding, strong characters and surprisingly grounded commentary on the impartial cruelty of many aspects of modern life; capitalism, poverty, war, y'know, the whole political commentary works. But the game's insights are heartfelt, and despite the setting being incredibly dark and cruel to its' inhabitants, the world has a tendency to instill a feeling of incredible, indomitable human will as you progress through its' story.

As for the story and narrative, I've already sung its' praises on a surface level but I feel simply leaving it at "its' good" doesn't do these elements the justice they deserve.

CP2077's story is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ excellent. The characters bring the colorful, unique and vibrant world to life in a very believable way, if you ask me. I didn't expect to find such strong and compelling personalities (especially for many characters that you don't even truly spend that much time with overall) in my campaign, but I was pleasantly surprised to find myself attached to many of the characters. Johnny Silverhand, Judy Alvarez, Panam Palmer, Goro Takemura, and Adam Smasher are particular favorites of mine, and all excellently written. Although I wish you saw more of them, Jackie Wells, Dexter Deshawn, River Ward and Evelyn Parker are also great characters. There are strong, recurring themes of hopelessness, exploitation, capitalistic indifference, and societal isolation, but also the indomitable human spirit, individuality, community and legacy. The game is also pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ funny when it wants to be.

Overall, I can't recommend this game enough, to be honest. One of the most shocking turnaround cases in video game history, and it is now one of my favorite games ever. None of this is to say the game is perfect in its' current state, it still has the odd bug here and there, mostly with the physics -- but rarely anything serious in my experience. My overall consideration of this game's rating will include Phantom Liberty by the way, totally worth it I think. Be warned that there's only one boss though, even though it is a pretty cool one. Nothing like anything else in the game, for sure! If you're looking for great Action RPG Shooter with a very well written story and world, great characters, and an incredibly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ jamming soundtrack, I would easily say Cyberpunk 2077 could be something you'd really enjoy.

Overall, love the game. Night city feels lived in, districts have distinct aesthetics, love the story, musics and the radios. However, I have some nitpicks, but they are not dealbreakers. I also would like to say that the DLC is far superior than the base game.

[b] Story: [/b]
It is good that you do not have to do side quests (NCPD, gigs) to move on the main story. However, the base game main story feels too short. I feel like cutting some side gigs in favor of focusing more of the main story would be better. Maybe even some bonding by doing some gigs together with Jackie pre-Konpeki Plaza to make his [spoiler] death [/spoiler] more impactful, instead of showing a quick cutscene.

Phantom Liberty is just flawless. Completing the DLC is so fullfilling because the story is just too good and its length just hit the spot. I like how the gigs intertwine with the main story just enough to not make it like a chore. Also, I love the horror section if you side with a certain character and would love to see more of those in the future game

[b] Gigs: [/b]
Most of the gigs in the base games are repetitive and bland, thus trying to complete all the gigs feels kind of like a chore. However, it never feels like a chore to do the gigs from Phantom Liberty and here are my reasonings.

First, we get to know characters in the gigs. We actively learn about their personality and their motive throughout the gigs. This makes the gigs more engaging.

This lead to the second point, where the gigs introduce you some moral dilemna. You are given differing options that actually impact the character differently. This make the gigs slighhtly personal because your choices and decisions matter and carry weight.

The impact of your choices can be experienced in the third point, which is by giving each gigs a conclusion in the form of mini side quest. In the base game, V complete their gigs no string attached. Sure V do not have to care about every single person they saved from a gig, but PL gives you the choice. You can either ignore the side quest, or if you are curious, you can follow through by completing the side quest.

So personally, I would love more moral dilemna in the future gigs. Although some days, I would also like some boring gigs like the one in the base game where I can just turn my brain off without having to spend 5 minutes arguing about morality. I guess 1 boring gig every 2 PL quality gig would be the sweet spot?

[b] Boss fight/Cyberpsychos on Very Hard: [/b]

Cyberpsychos are too squishies. I feel like it is reasonable to increase their durability by 50%. However, only making the fight longer will not be fun. They also need more movesets because currently they feel too predictable and telegraphic. Fighting a melee as a melee is only fun for the few seconds because they will just repeat the same move over and over again. This make the fight bland where you just stand still > wait for enemy to lunge attack > Parry > Hack and slash, then repeat the process.

Love the boss fights, especially the Kurt Hansen one. He has the perfect amount of health, movesets and different QTE (or mini cutscene? I forgot). My only complain is the hp for Chimera and Adam Smasher. Fighting the Chimera is very exciting because you can die quickly if you are not careful. However, once you learn how to avoid the attacks, the fight overstays its welcome due to the massive health pool. It is not fun to run and hide for 15 seconds straight only to then fire a few rounds, then repeat the same process over 15 times or even more. Maybe my gun sucked. Would be nice to have the Chimera and Adam Smasher health reduced by 1/3 personally.

[b] Romance: [/b]

The romance with the female characters are amazing because they are fleshed-out. Wish I could say the same for the male counterpart though. I love the decision of making them having specific sexual preference instead of player sexual because it does make the world more realistic. However, this would be better there were more options for romance. Maybe then you can add some playersexual in the mix too. Anyways it was a mistake to scrape of Takemura romance.

For PL, not being able to romance Alex and Aurore is such a big missed opportunity. Their characters are important in the story that their romance might introduce new options regarding their fate, and amplify the impact of their fate.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a game I ended up spending way more time on than I originally planned. Night City is still interesting to explore, especially when you stop following only the main story and start clearing side jobs, activities, and random events.

I went through almost all of the main game, and with Phantom Liberty there is more than enough content. I liked the DLC, especially its separate story, new characters, and the different atmosphere of Dogtown. Some of the side quests in the base game are also surprisingly memorable.

There are quite a few different endings, and you shouldn't really expect a typical happy ending. Depending on your choices, things can turn out very differently, and some of the endings are pretty harsh. I think that fits the Cyberpunk setting quite well.

There are also plenty of ways to build your character. Out of all the cyberware and different builds, Sandevistan was probably my favorite. Slowing down time and taking out enemies up close never really got old. You can also focus on guns, stealth, hacking, or mix different playstyles together.

After playing for a lot of hours, some activities definitely start to feel repetitive, and a few mechanics could have been deeper. There are also still some small bugs and weird moments from time to time, although I never had anything serious that actually stopped me from playing.

And the radio deserves a mention too. I listened to 98.7 Body Heat a lot while driving around Night City, and *Who's Ready for Tomorrow* fits the atmosphere perfectly.

Overall, I enjoyed it. After finishing almost everything the game has to offer, I'd say Cyberpunk 2077 is a really solid RPG, but I wouldn't call it perfect. The city, characters, music, and Phantom Liberty all work well together, and in the end it mostly comes down to whether you like the setting and the kind of game it is.

After years of hearing about this game's absolute flop of a launch, and how it's "better now", I finally bought the game and played it. This is one of the best games I think I've ever played. So many parts of this game feel so alive and soulful. You can absolutely see the heart the devs put into the game over the years, and as of the current update (2.31), it feels truly complete. 

The main story is somewhat short after act I ends, but with the intrigue and all sorts of gigs and jobs the world presents to you, it's rare to find yourself actually doing the main story with how much there is to do.  

I will admit there are still a fair amount of bugs and kind of issues I ran into throughout the game. Multiple times when calling my car, it would be flipped upside down, clipped into the ground, or one time it even just fell through the ground into the abyss. Aside from that the game played flawlessly and looked great even at lower settings. 

V and Johnny are in my opinion, such amazing characters, V really feels like an outlet into night city. V is already their own character, but there's enough variation in dialogue options and V's lifepath that your V feels like YOUR V.

Phantom liberty as well was such a trip. A lot of the gigs you get are similar to the main game's ones, but the main story takes on a different kind of story style which personally, I didn't think the game would take. It absolutely fit with the story of the game as well as the themes, so it's absolutely worth the money if you can get it, plus a lot of the weapons you can get out of it are so fun and useful. 

After the endings of both the main game and the DLC, I just had to sit there and just process what I played. None of it was because the ending I had gotten was bad, but because I wondered if there was anything I could had done to make things better for these characters, but as the game tells you. 

In Night City, there are no happy endings.

Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition — 4.5/5

Finished every ending, and honestly, I still think the Arasaka ending from the base game is the strongest one. Not necessarily because it is the nicest, but because it feels the most Cyberpunk. The quality, the atmosphere, the way it leaves you sitting there for a minute after the credits — it just fits this world perfectly.

Phantom Liberty is great too. It adds a cool new storyline, memorable characters, and another possible ending. But I personally don’t really understand the more “happy ending” direction. In a world like Cyberpunk, I don’t think a truly good ending should exist. It makes things feel a little less brutal and believable to me — although that may just be my own problem with it.

Also, I need to mention that one DLC section where you have to run from the robot: I was so annoyed I genuinely considered dropping the game. Absolute nightmare fuel, not in a fun way.

Still, the game itself was nearly perfect for me. It ran flawlessly from start to finish: no bugs, no crashes, no weird technical problems. The graphics are insane and probably among the best I’ve seen in any game. Night City’s lighting is on another level, and the music constantly makes even a simple drive through the city feel important.

Base game: 4.5/5
Phantom Liberty: 4/5
Ultimate Edition overall: 4.5/5

The worldbuilding of Cyberpunk 2077 alone justifies buying this game. Cyberpunk does an amazing job of letting the world speak for itself on themes that are incredibly relevant in the modern day, such as the effects of corporatism on society, the implications of artificial intelligence, and touches even on mass surveillance and climate change, through the primary narrative of V's story, the various side quests, or the environmental storytelling from various items and story bits scattered around the map. Outside of its commentary, all the elements within the game, from body modifications and cyberpsychos to the way the encounters and city are set up just "make sense" in a cohesive way. The more you explore Night City, the more real it feels, which is an impressive feat for a game of this scope.

Outside of this, Cyberpunk does an amazing job of getting you invested with the main characters of the story, all of which are incredibly fleshed out with their own nuances and personalities. The atmosphere of the game is incredible: I've often stayed up late at night without realizing it because I got too invested in driving down the main highways at night with Body Rock Radio blasting in the background.

The passion and attention to detail that CD PROJEKT RED has put in this game makes Cyberpunk 2077 a masterpiece of both the open world and cyberpunk genres. What an incredible ride, and what an incredible labor of love.

There seems to be a lot of things you can do, but I can't really judge that, since I've only played it a little and couldn't properly explore the entire game. Story overall also looks promising, although I can't really judge that either with 8 hours of gameplay.

Cons:
Now to the cons, which for me are currently overweighting the cons. The game feels clunky. The driving is awful, it is probably the worst driving I've seen so far, feeling even worse than FC3, which already was a pain in the ass for me. The gunplay is massively underwhelming in my opinion. Like how the hell am I dumping 3 shotgun mags into someone's head and they are still alive? Enemies are extreme bullet sponges and that just ruins the experience for me. Also, the guns feel really unresponsive and the melee is just sliding around the room, slashing at people without much depth. The dialogues are really long and "draggy". The quests so far have not really felt rewarding and were rather boring. Some of the mechanics, like braindancing, were just straight up immersion-breaking for me. It took so long to finish the first braindance quest that I straight up don't want to ever experience it again. It was an interesting idea, I don't deny that, but overall it just feels dull. 

With that being said, I currently can't recommend the game. I wish I could give it a neutral score, especially since I can see the good things it has to offer. I really wanted to give it a shot and like the game, but I currently don't have enough time on my hands to force myself into playing a game that doesn't really entertain me, hoping it gets better soon. It is my personal preference though and I can deffinitely see why some people love this game so much. For me, it just didn't feel worth to continue.

I am a huge CDPR fan, especially because of The Witcher games, in which I've invested hunderds of hours across different platforms, but these games just felt rewarding, the story was gripping, the setting was even better (for me personally) and I didn't mind spending so much time on it. With Cyberpunk2077 I can't really say the same. Chances are that I will eventually change my review later, if I ever get to a point of giving it another shot, in the future, but currently I will just leave it be.

⭐ Steam Review: Cyberpunk 2077 + Phantom Liberty
Cyberpunk 2077 in 2026 is basically a completely different game from the one we got at launch — and honestly, it’s one of the best redemption arcs in gaming. Night City finally feels alive, dangerous, stylish, and worth getting lost in.

The base game’s story still hits hard: V’s struggle, Johnny’s chaos, the character arcs with Panam, Judy, Takemura — they’re all still some of the best narrative work in any RPG. But the real magic now is how the systems finally support the fantasy. Combat is smoother, builds actually matter, vehicles feel better, cops exist (mostly), and the city doesn’t feel like it’s held together with duct tape anymore.

Phantom Liberty takes all of that and injects a shot of adrenaline straight into the game. Dogtown is grimy, dense, and hostile in a way the rest of Night City never quite was. The spy‑thriller tone is a perfect contrast to the main story, and Idris Elba’s performance as Solomon Reed is ridiculously good. The expansion’s quests are tight, intense, and full of choices that actually feel heavy — including an ending that completely rewrites the fate of V.

The new skill trees and cyberware changes make builds way more fun. You can actually play the game how you want: stealthy netrunner, chrome‑maxed berserker, smart‑gun tactician, katana demon — whatever. It finally feels like an RPG instead of a shooter with stats.

Is it perfect? No. Some jank still pops up, and the open world can feel empty in spots. But the difference between launch Cyberpunk and current Cyberpunk is night and day.

If you bounced off the game years ago, it’s absolutely worth coming back.
If you’re new, you’re getting the definitive version.

Cyberpunk 2077 + Phantom Liberty is stylish, emotional, chaotic, and unforgettable.
A flawed masterpiece that finally lives up to its potential.

I Can’t Move On From Night City

CD Projekt Red created a beautifully crafted piece of ART called Cyberpunk 2077. The kind of experience that lingers long after you’ve stepped away. The last time something hit me this hard emotionally was Red Dead Redemption 2, back in 2022. And now, years later, Cyberpunk 2077 has done it again.

The city itself is a character. Towering megabuildings, rain-slicked alleys, neon bleeding into concrete- every district has its own pulse, its own danger, its own beauty. The NCPD variations, the climate design, the sheer density of detail packed into every corner of this world - it’s all top-tier. You don’t just visit Night City. You breathe it in.

It starts deceptively light - heists, gigs, exploring the sprawl, making a few cool friends along the way. But as you go deeper, the tone shifts. It stops being about thriving and starts being about surviving. Every morning becomes a quiet question: how many more days do I get in this city? That shift- from ambition to survival- is where this experience stops being fun and starts being unforgettable.

And at the center of it all: Keanu Reeves as Johnny Silverhand. Once again, he delivers a career-defining, breathtaking performance - reckless, wounded, magnetic. The man is a legend of our generation, and this role proves it all over again.

But Johnny isn’t alone in carrying this story. Every character you meet leaves a mark. Jackie’s loyalty. Panam’s fire. Judy’s quiet resilience. Viktor’s steady hands and steadier heart. Rogue’s legend. Each one doesn’t just support the story- they challenge you, forcing real decisions with real consequences. These characters aren’t just good. They’re some of the greatest ever written.

By the end, Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t something you finish. It’s a world you mourn leaving.

Final Scores:

* Story: 9/10
* Characters: 9.5/10
* World Building: 10/10
* Attention to Detail: 10/10
* Environment Design: 10/10
* Lighting: 10/10

I wanted to wait until I got to one of the endings to write this review. And yeah, I know about how awful the launch of this game was, but this game has had a recovery unlike any I've ever seen. Never have I resonated so hard with the messages a game has tried to deliver, and so many things about this game are relevant today, from the AI enshittification of everything we know and love, to katanas still being freakin awesome. I have a solid amount of hours by this point and that number will only continue to go up, so I wanna talk about some pros and cons in case you're considering buying this game for yourself or someone else. 

PROS: 
- Immersive open world with each location being distinctly different from the last. (i found myself spending several hours just driving around listening to the radio and just taking everything in).
- absolutely stellar animation and voice work, i literally forgot i was playing a game at certain points throughout
- fulfilling combat/stealth mechanics with there always being creative ways to enter buildings or complete objectives based on your stat spread, and there being so many different ways to take down enemies rather than just point-and-shoot.
- Outstanding visual presentation - exceptional graphics, especially on modern PCs and current-generation consoles.
- Upgrading actually feels integral to the story, installing cybernetic enhancements feels meaningful and changes gameplay considerably.
I could go on and on, but you should play it for yourself to see the rest. 

CONS (imo): 
- Loot can become overwhelming. Equipment management can often require frequent sorting and dismantling.
- Romance options (because I know what kind of people some of you are) are well-written but relatively few. Relationships get extremely stale after their main questline ends. 
- Money becomes plentiful in the mid-to-late game, reducing the importance of financial decisions (unless you blow it all on vending machines and gambling, i guess)
- While dialogue choices matter in some situations, the central narrative is relatively linear compared to some classic RPGs.
- The three origins you get (Nomad, Streetkid, and Corpo) mostly affect early-game content and dialogue rather than significantly altering the overall experience.

Overall, I still rate this game as one of my favorites of all time, and highly suggest you check it out for yourself. Wake tf up, Samurai. You have a game to play.

101 hours. Cyberpunk finally defeated me.

I got a lot out of this game, and when Cyberpunk is good, it can be really fun. The combat is great, building out your character and cyberware is addictive, and a lot of the gigs and side missions were easily my favorite parts of the game. They were quick, gave you an objective, let you approach it your way, and then got the hell out of your way.

Unfortunately, once I started focusing on the main story, I hit a wall.

The pacing is absolutely exhausting. Walk with somebody. Listen to them talk. Get in a car. Listen to them talk. Follow somebody. Listen to them talk. Sit down. Listen to them talk. Repeat.

Some of these sequences feel like they go on for 20–30 minutes, and because the game is committed to first person, so much of the storytelling is literally just standing there staring at another character while they dump dialogue on you. There aren't interesting camera angles or cinematic cuts to keep scenes visually engaging. You're just trapped in V's head waiting for people to finish talking.

The braindance sequences were especially miserable for me, and I hated how often the game takes control and momentum away from you for scripted rides, conversations, slow walks, scanning, following characters, and other sequences where you're technically "playing" but barely doing anything.

That's what makes it frustrating, because underneath all of that is a game I actually enjoyed. I loved sneaking into buildings, hacking cameras, throwing knives, using suppressed pistols, upgrading cyberware, experimenting with quickhacks, buying ridiculous cars, and figuring out different ways to clear an objective. When Cyberpunk lets me play Cyberpunk, I like Cyberpunk.

But eventually I realized I was spending too much of my time waiting to get back to the parts I enjoyed.

I even tried Phantom Liberty, unlocked the Relic tree, entered Dogtown, and almost immediately found myself thinking, oh God, more walking and talking.

I wanted to finish the main story. I really did. After 101 hours, I figured I had to. But gaming shouldn't feel like homework, and eventually I realized I was forcing myself to finish something I wasn't enjoying anymore.

So I'm calling it.

Great world. Great combat. Great character-building. Some genuinely fun side content. Terrible pacing, overly long dialogue sequences, too many moments where control is taken away from the player, and storytelling that I found incredibly stale.

After 101 hours, Cyberpunk didn't beat V.

It beat me.

4/10 — Not Recommended.
