Cyberpunk 2077 isn't a perfect game. It's my favorite game. There's a difference.

I've spent hundreds of hours in Night City across different playthroughs, even if Steam only accounts for part of that time, replayed the game, explored its streets, read its lore, finished its quests, got attached to its characters, and somehow I still get that feeling when I'm just driving through the city at night with the radio playing.

That's what makes Cyberpunk special to me. Night City doesn't feel like a map built around the player. It feels like a place that existed before V and will continue existing after V is gone. Every district has its own identity, history and people. You can walk past some random alley, read a shard or find a small environmental story, and suddenly understand a little more about the kind of world you're living in.

And the characters are probably what I love most. Johnny, Judy, Panam, Reed, Songbird, Jackie (my poor amigo), Viktor, Misty, Kerry and so many others aren't just NPCs handing you quests. You build relationships with them. You disagree with them. Sometimes you help them, sometimes you hurt them, and sometimes there simply isn't a good answer. Eventually they become part of your version of V's story.

That's also why I love the choices in this game. Cyberpunk doesn't constantly put a giant “THIS DECISION WILL HAVE CONSEQUENCES” sign on the screen. Sometimes a dialogue choice changes a relationship. Sometimes something you did hours ago comes back. Sometimes your choices don't change the world at all—and that's kind of the point. Night City is bigger than you.

Phantom Liberty somehow made all of this even better. It gave me another cast of characters I genuinely cared about and put me into situations where I understood multiple sides while knowing somebody was probably going to get destroyed by whatever I chose. Reed and Songbird especially are characters I could talk about for hours.

The gameplay is great. The builds are fun. The guns, cyberware, cars, music and visuals are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ incredible. But none of those things individually explain why I have this much attachment to Cyberpunk.

It's the combination:

Characters + relationships + worldbuilding + lore + choices + quests + exploration + atmosphere.

There are games with bigger maps. There are games with more choices. There are games with deeper RPG systems. There are probably games that do individual parts of Cyberpunk better.

But I've never played another game where all of those things came together in a way that affected me quite like this.

And yes, I remember the launch. I know how broken it was. CDPR deserved the criticism they received for releasing the game in that state, especially on last-gen consoles. I'm not going to rewrite history just because I love what the game eventually became.

But I'm reviewing the game I've actually spent all these years playing.

And that game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ phenomenal.

Mike Pondsmith created one hell of a universe, and CDPR made me feel like I actually lived in a small piece of it.

When the credits roll, I don't feel like I'm finished with an open-world game.

I feel like I'm leaving Night City.

And apparently I'm terrible at leaving, because I always ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ come back.

Great Gameplay, Incredible Characters, Missed Potential

Great gameplay, great characters, and a good story. Cyberpunk 2077 was an incredibly fun game for me, mainly because of its gameplay. I love how fast and thrilling the combat can be, while still allowing you to approach encounters stealthily and methodically. There are so many different playstyles and possibilities that, at times, it gets close to a true immersive sim like Deus Ex.

At first, driving felt frustrating. Cars and bikes don’t turn particularly well and can take a lot of space to brake. It feels somewhat realistic, but not always fun. However, I quickly got used to it, and eventually I actually started enjoying it. I found myself looking for better vehicles and choosing to drive instead of fast traveling. Compared to GTA V, where the amount of driving eventually becomes tedious, I actually looked forward to getting behind the wheel here.

The retrofuturistic car designs are fantastic and fit the game's aesthetic perfectly. The sound design deserves a special mention too—the engine noises, induction sounds, and gear changes are incredibly satisfying and make the vehicles feel surprisingly authentic.

The story is good, but for me, it’s carried by its fantastic cast of characters and performances. I especially loved Female V's voice acting. Most of the main characters feel fleshed out and receive meaningful development throughout the game.

This is where Phantom Liberty really stood out to me. Its storyline is easily one of the best parts of the entire game. The performances are incredible, the characters are more compelling, and, most importantly, your decisions can have genuinely meaningful consequences. I loved how the expansion gives you choices that don't just change dialogue, but can significantly affect how the story unfolds. Its final stretch and the different outcomes were some of the most memorable moments of my entire playthrough.

My biggest problem is the open world. Night City looks incredible, but I don't think it offers enough interactivity or meaningful exploration. I also wish the world-building had been stronger. Compared to The Witcher 3, which makes exploration feel like an adventure in itself, Cyberpunk falls behind.

I also found the pacing uneven. The beginning is quite slow, while the story starts moving almost too quickly toward the end. I particularly felt that the Aldecaldos storyline could have used more time to develop. Interestingly, Phantom Liberty felt much more focused and consistently paced to me, which made the contrast even more noticeable.

Performance was generally good for me, but I did experience some crashes on my RX 9070, along with a few strange graphical glitches.

Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a great game with fantastic gameplay, characters, and presentation. Phantom Liberty shows just how good this world can be when CD Projekt Red is firing on all cylinders, especially when it comes to writing, character development, performances, and meaningful choices. The open-world design and uneven pacing keep it from being perfect for me, but this is still an incredible experience that I absolutely recommend.
